# How to use this subject

Cosmetics and Cosmeceuticals (MPH204T) is the second-semester M.Pharm Pharmaceutics course that turns formulation science into consumer products: creams, shampoos, toothpastes, sunscreens and herbal cosmetics. Unlike the B.Pharm elective Cosmetic Science (BP809ET), the M.Pharm paper expects you to **quote the law rule by rule**, **explain the biology behind each skin, hair or oral problem**, **justify every ingredient in a formula**, and **discuss safety, regulation and current controversies** (parabens, formaldehyde releasers, 1,4-dioxane, fragrance allergens, natural standards).

## Units and how they map to the PCI syllabus

The five units follow the five units of the PCI MPH 204T syllabus exactly (60 hours, 12 hours each).

| Unit | PCI syllabus unit | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | Cosmetics – Regulatory | Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940 and Cosmetics Rules, 2020: definition, labelling, import, misbranded/spurious (and adulterated), manufacture, loan licence, prohibitions, offences and penalties |
| 2 | Cosmetics – Biological aspects | Skin problems (dry skin, acne, pigmentation, prickly heat, wrinkles, body odour), hair structure and growth cycle, oral problems, care needs of each body region |
| 3 | Formulation building blocks | Surfactants, emollients, rheology modifiers, preservatives and their efficacy, classic product formulas, soaps and syndets, perfumes and EU allergens, controversial ingredients. The largest unit |
| 4 | Design of cosmeceutical products | Sunscreens and their regulation, then product design for each problem. A section on **safety, stability and efficacy evaluation** has been added here because it is needed to answer "design" questions fully and is part of the course objectives (safety, stability and efficacy) |
| 5 | Herbal cosmetics | Herbal ingredients for hair, skin and oral care; COSMOS rules for preservatives, emollients, foaming agents, emulsifiers and rheology modifiers; challenges |

The related B.Pharm pack (BP809ET Cosmetic Science) covers the same basics at a simpler level and has practical guides; use it for quick revision of definitions, SPF and BIS tests.

## Exam pattern

The paper carries **100 marks: 25 internal assessment + 75 end-semester**, and the end-semester examination lasts **3 hours**. PCI does not prescribe a section-wise pattern for M.Pharm, so most universities follow the PCI B.Pharm 75-mark split shown below (used for M.Pharm by, for example, Bahra University, Shimla). Confirm the exact pattern with your university.

| Section | What it asks | Marks |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A | Objective / MCQ, all compulsory | 20 × 1 = 20 |
| B | Long essays – attempt 2 of 3 | 2 × 10 = 20 |
| C | Short answers – attempt 7 of 9 | 7 × 5 = 35 |
| | Total | 75 |

The question bank has long (10-mark), short (5-mark) and very short (2-mark) questions for every unit. The mock paper uses the pattern above, and a 20-question, 20-minute MCQ test is included for quick practice.

## Probability ratings

- **High** – a frequent question type for this syllabus topic; prepare a full answer with tables and examples.
- **Medium** – appears every few years or as part of a bigger question.
- **Low** – rare; useful for MCQs and as a backup choice.

The ratings are estimates from syllabus weight and common question patterns in PCI-syllabus pharmacy papers. They are not a promise of what will be asked.

## Where the marks usually come from

| Unit | Topics that keep coming back |
| --- | --- |
| 1 | Definition of cosmetic (section 3(aaa)) with analysis; labelling requirements; import registration and prohibitions; misbranded vs spurious vs adulterated; conditions for a manufacturing licence; loan licence; penalties |
| 2 | Skin structure and barrier; acne pathogenesis; melanogenesis; hair structure and growth cycle; dental caries and sensitivity; body odour |
| 3 | Classification of surfactants with HLB; preservatives – merits/demerits and factors affecting efficacy; formulas of vanishing cream, cold cream, shampoo, toothpaste; soap vs syndet; perfume classification; parabens, formaldehyde releasers, dioxane |
| 4 | Classification of sunscreens, SPF and UVA rating, sunscreen regulation; formulating for acne, pigmentation, wrinkles, dandruff; antiperspirant vs deodorant; desensitising and anti-caries toothpastes |
| 5 | Herbal ingredients in hair/skin/oral care with constituents; COSMOS standard; challenges of herbal cosmetics |

## Scoring tips for this subject

1. **Law answers:** always cite the source – "section 3(aaa) of the Act", "Rule 34 of the Cosmetics Rules, 2020", "Form COS-8". Name the authority (CDSCO/CLA vs State Licensing Authority) and give the time limits (45 days, 30 days, six months, five years). A table of "item – requirement – rule" scores well.
2. **Biology answers:** draw the skin cross-section, the acne cascade, the melanin pathway and the hair-growth cycle as labelled text diagrams. Link each to a cosmeceutical approach in one line – examiners at M.Pharm level reward this connection.
3. **Formulation answers:** write a formula table with **ingredient – function – typical %**, then the method (phase temperatures, order of mixing) and evaluation tests. Explain *why* (e.g. why stearic acid gives a pearly vanishing cream, why calcium carbonate pastes use monofluorophosphate).
4. **Comparison tables** make strong short answers: soap vs syndet, cold vs vanishing cream, organic vs inorganic sunscreen, deodorant vs antiperspirant, licence vs loan licence, misbranded vs spurious vs adulterated, intrinsic vs extrinsic ageing, COSMOS ORGANIC vs NATURAL.
5. **Controversy questions:** give hazard, exposure, risk and the current regulatory position (EU limits for parabens; 0.001% "releases formaldehyde" warning; dioxane as an ethoxylation impurity controlled by stripping). End with the formulator's balanced view.
6. **Numbers to remember:** acid mantle pH 4.5–5.5; SPF at 2 mg/cm²; λc ≥ 370 nm; UVA-PF ≥ ⅓ SPF; fluoride ≤ 1000 ppm; TFM 76/70/60%; allergen labelling 0.001%/0.01%; COSMOS 20%/10%, 95% PPAI, 2% petrochemical; mercury 70 ppm/1 ppm; colours As 2 ppm, Pb 20 ppm; MoS ≥ 100.
7. Do not invent rule numbers, fines or dates in the exam. If unsure, describe the provision in words – you lose fewer marks than for a wrong number.

# Last-night revision sheet — MPH204T

## Unit 1: Regulation

- Cosmetic (section 3(aaa), D&C Act 1940): rubbed, poured, sprinkled, sprayed, introduced into or applied to the human body for cleansing, beautifying, promoting attractiveness, altering appearance; includes components. Disease or body-function claim → drug.
- Cosmetics Rules, 2020: G.S.R. 763(E), 15 Dec 2020; replaced Form 32, Schedule M-II, Schedule S of the 1945 Rules. CLA (CDSCO) = import, new cosmetics; SLA = manufacture, sale.
- New cosmetic = novel ingredient; COS-12 → COS-3; safety tests per IS 4011:2018.
- Import: COS-1 → COS-2 (within 6 months; perpetual with retention fee every 5 years; 2%/month late fee up to 180 days). Registered product imported by others: COS-4 → COS-4A (3 years). Changes reported in 15 days; constitution change → fresh registration in 180 days.
- Import bans (Rule 18): banned in country of origin; use-before ≤ 6 months from import; hexachlorophene; tested on animals after 12 Nov 2014. Personal-use baggage allowed.
- Manufacture: COS-5 / COS-6 (loan) + COS-7 GMP self-declaration → COS-8 / COS-9 in 45 days; upload on CDSCO site; SLA inspects within 30 days; inspection at least once in 3 years (risk-based).
- Technical person (whole-time): D.Pharm / registered pharmacist / Intermediate with chemistry / B. Cosmetic Technology. Test every batch of raw material and product (own lab or NABL-accredited approved lab). Batch records 3 years after expiry. Changes reported in 30 days. Constitution change: licence valid max 6 months.
- Loan licence: use another licensee's site; COS-9 falls with the host's COS-8.
- Label (Rule 34): name; manufacturer and address; use before; batch "B."; licence "M."; net contents (outer); hazards; INGREDIENTS > 1% in descending order; imports "RC No." + importer; stickering in bonded warehouse. Hair dye caution + 24 h patch test (Rule 37); fluoride ≤ 1000 ppm (Rule 38).
- 17C misbranded (wrong label/colour/claim), 17D spurious (wrong identity), 17E adulterated (filthy, insanitary, poisonous container, non-permitted colour, harmful substance). Section 18 prohibitions; 27A: spurious/adulterated up to 3 years + fine; others up to 1 year or fine.
- Rule 39: BIS standards; IS 4707 Part 2 Annex A banned; colours Tenth Schedule (As 2 ppm, Pb 20 ppm, heavy metals 100 ppm); hexachlorophene only soap ≤ 1%; mercury 70 ppm (eye) / 1 ppm; no lead/arsenic colours; no animal testing.

## Unit 2: Biology

- Stratum corneum bricks (corneocytes) + mortar (ceramides, cholesterol, FFA); NMF from filaggrin (amino acids, PCA, lactate, urea); TEWL; acid mantle pH 4.5–5.5.
- Dry skin: lipid/NMF loss → abnormal desquamation. Acne: sebum, hyperkeratinisation, C. acnes, inflammation.
- Melanin: tyrosine → DOPA → dopaquinone (tyrosinase) → eumelanin / pheomelanin; UV → α-MSH → MC1R; melasma, PIH, lentigines.
- Miliaria: blocked eccrine ducts – crystallina, rubra, profunda. Photoageing: UV → ROS → MMPs; glycation.
- Body odour: apocrine secretion + Corynebacterium/Staphylococcus → 3-methyl-2-hexenoic acid, thioalcohols.
- Hair: cuticle/cortex/medulla; disulphide, hydrogen, salt bonds; IEP about 3.7; negative charge; anagen 2–7 y, catagen 2–3 wk, telogen ~3 mo. Dandruff = Malassezia; AGA = DHT.
- Teeth: caries below pH ~5.5; gingivitis from plaque; halitosis = VSCs; sensitivity = hydrodynamic theory.

## Unit 3: Building blocks

- Surfactants: anionic (SLS, SLES, SCI, soaps), cationic (quats – conditioners, CPC), amphoteric (CAPB), non-ionic (polysorbates, ethoxylates, APGs). HLB 3–6 w/o, 8–18 o/w, 15–18 solubilisers; packing parameter.
- Emollients: hydrocarbons (petrolatum most occlusive), triglycerides, esters, fatty alcohols/acids, silicones, lanolin, waxes, ceramides.
- Rheology: gums, cellulose ethers, carbomers (neutralise), associative, NaCl for shampoos, clays/silica, fatty alcohols. Shear-thinning + yield value.
- Preservative efficacy: pH/pKa, partition, non-ionic binding, interactions, packaging, aw, load, structure, synergy (EDTA). Challenge test ISO 11930: P. aeruginosa, S. aureus, E. coli, C. albicans, A. brasiliensis, 28 days.
- Vanishing cream: stearic acid 15–25% partly neutralised → o/w, matt, pearly. Cold cream: beeswax + borax + mineral oil + water → w/o, cooling.
- Shampoo: SLES + CAPB + polyquaternium + salt + pearliser + ZPT; coacervate. Toothpaste: abrasive + humectant + binder + SLS + fluoride + flavour; CaCO3 with MFP.
- Soap pH 9–10, scum, TFM 76/70/60%; syndet (SCI) pH 5.5–7, mild; combars.
- Perfume: origin, families (floral, fresh, oriental, woody, chypre, fougère), concentration (parfum 20–30%, EDP 15–20%, EDT 5–15%, cologne 2–5%), notes top/heart/base; IFRA.
- EU allergens: 26 (24 chemicals + oakmoss, treemoss), label > 0.001% leave-on, > 0.01% rinse-off; expanded to ~80 (Reg. 2023/1545); HICC, atranol, chloroatranol, lilial banned.
- Parabens: methyl/ethyl 0.4% single / 0.8% mix; propyl + butyl ≤ 0.14%, not in nappy-area leave-on < 3 y; 5 parabens banned. Formaldehyde releasers: "releases formaldehyde" > 0.001% (Reg. 2022/1181). 1,4-Dioxane: ethoxylation by-product; vacuum stripping.

## Unit 4: Cosmeceutical design and evaluation

- UVB 290–320, UVA2 320–340, UVA1 340–400 nm. Organic filters (octinoxate, octisalate, homosalate, octocrylene, oxybenzone, avobenzone, bemotrizinol, bisoctrizole, ecamsule) vs inorganic (ZnO, TiO2).
- SPF = MED protected/unprotected at 2 mg/cm² (ISO 24444); SPF 15/30/50 ≈ 93/97/98% UVB; λc ≥ 370 nm; EU UVA-PF ≥ ⅓ SPF, bands low/medium/high/very high; PA+ to PA++++ (PPD 2/4/8/16). India & EU cosmetic; USA OTC drug.
- Dry skin: glycerin, urea, PCA, HA + petrolatum/dimethicone + ceramide–cholesterol–FFA + niacinamide.
- Acne: salicylic acid, niacinamide, zinc, retinol, non-comedogenic gels. Pigmentation: kojic acid, arbutin, glabridin, vitamin C, niacinamide (transfer), sunscreen + iron oxides.
- Wrinkles: retinol, vitamin C/E, ferulic acid, peptides, AHAs, HA, sunscreen. Prickly heat: talc/starch + ZnO/calamine + menthol.
- Deodorant (antimicrobial, fragrance, zinc ricinoleate) vs antiperspirant (aluminium chlorohydrate plugs ducts). Dandruff: ZPT, piroctone olamine, climbazole, selenium sulphide.
- Oral: fluoride (NaF, MFP, SnF2); gums: SnF2, zinc citrate, CPC, essential oils; halitosis: zinc, CPC, ClO2; sensitivity: KNO3 (nerve), SnF2/strontium/arginine/bioactive glass (occlusion).
- Safety: MoS = NOAEL/SED ≥ 100; OECD 439 (irritation), 431 (corrosion), 437 BCOP/492 (eye), 442C/D/E (sensitisation), 432 (phototox), 428 (absorption); HRIPT; IS 4011:2018.
- Efficacy: corneometer, TEWL, sebumeter, cutometer, chromameter/Mexameter, profilometry, combing force; claims truthful (Rule 36).

## Unit 5: Herbal cosmetics

- Hair: amla, bhringraj (wedelolactone), hibiscus, henna (lawsone), shikakai/reetha (saponins), neem, methi, rosemary, aloe.
- Skin: turmeric (curcumin), aloe, neem, sandalwood (santalols), saffron (crocin), liquorice (glabridin), green tea (EGCG), centella (asiaticoside), papaya (papain), tea tree (terpinen-4-ol), rose, multani mitti.
- Oral: neem, babool (tannins), clove (eugenol), miswak (Salvadora persica), mint, thyme (thymol), liquorice, bakul.
- No legal "herbal/natural/organic" definition in Indian cosmetic law; Ayurvedic with medicinal claims = ASU drug. ISO 16128 indices.
- COSMOS (BDIH, Cosmebio, Ecocert, ICEA, Soil Association): ORGANIC ≥ 20% organic (≥ 10% rinse-off/aqueous/mineral-rich), ≥ 95% PPAI organic, ≤ 2% petrochemical moieties; NATURAL; CERTIFIED and APPROVED raw materials. No ethoxylation/propoxylation, GMO, irradiation, mineral oil, silicones.
- COSMOS preservatives: organic acids + salts (benzoic, sorbic, dehydroacetic, salicylic), benzyl alcohol; not parabens, formaldehyde releasers, isothiazolinones, phenoxyethanol. Emulsifiers: glyceryl stearate, sucrose/polyglyceryl esters, glucosides, olivates, lecithin. Foamers: APGs, glutamates, betaines, saponins, soaps. Thickeners: xanthan, guar, gellan, clays.
- Challenges: variability, adulteration, microbes, preservation, heavy metals/pesticides, stability, colour/odour, solubility, sensory, allergens and phototoxicity, evidence, regulation, sustainability.

questions.answer:
1. Definition – section 3(aaa): any article intended to be rubbed, poured, sprinkled or sprayed on, introduced into or otherwise applied to the human body or any part of it for cleansing, beautifying, promoting attractiveness or altering the appearance; includes any article meant as a component of a cosmetic. Intended use and claims decide status; a disease or body-function claim makes it a drug.
2. Authority – State Licensing Authority (state drugs controller) licenses manufacture; CLA (CDSCO) grants prior permission for a new cosmetic (COS-12 → COS-3).
3. Application (Rule 23) – online in Form COS-5 (licence) or COS-6 (loan licence) with fee (Third Schedule), documents (Second Schedule Part II) and a self-declaration in Form COS-7 of compliance with GMP, premises, plant and equipment (Seventh Schedule).
4. Grant – licence in Form COS-8 (loan licence COS-9) within 45 days; licence uploaded on CDSCO website before manufacture; SLA inspects within 30 days to verify COS-7; if not inspected in time the licence is deemed valid; false declaration → show cause, cancellation or stop-work.
5. Separate licence for each premises (Rule 24); rejection with reasons, re-application within six months, appeal to State Government within 90 days.
6. Conditions (Rule 26): manufacture under a whole-time competent technical person (D.Pharm / registered pharmacist / Intermediate with chemistry / degree in cosmetic technology); premises as per Seventh Schedule; testing of each batch of raw material and finished product in own lab or an approved NABL-accredited lab; test records 3 years from manufacture; batch records (Eighth Schedule) kept 3 years after expiry; inspectors allowed to inspect and sample (COS-10); inspection book COS-11; changes in labelling/composition/testing reported within 30 days with undertaking of BIS compliance; change in constitution – licence valid at most 6 months; change of name/address approved within 60 days. Soap makers exempt from testing/document clauses.
7. Validity (Rule 30) – perpetual, subject to retention fee every five years (late fee 2% per month up to 180 days, then deemed cancelled).
8. Inspection at least once in three years or risk-based (Rule 31).
questions.question: Define a cosmetic as per the Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940. Describe the regulatory provisions under the Cosmetics Rules, 2020 for obtaining a licence to manufacture cosmetics, including the conditions of licence.

questions.answer:
1. Registration compulsory (Rule 12): no cosmetic imported unless registered by the Central Licensing Authority (CDSCO).
2. Applicant: the manufacturer, its authorised Indian agent, the importer, or its Indian subsidiary; online Form COS-1 with documents (Second Schedule Part I) and fee per category per site; authorisation authenticated before a first-class magistrate or competent foreign authority.
3. Bulk ready-to-fill formulations also need an Indian manufacturing licence for filling and brand owner details.
4. Testing of identified products at an approved laboratory; inspection of foreign site if needed (at applicant's cost).
5. Grant (Rule 13): import registration certificate Form COS-2 or rejection with reasons within 6 months; appeal to Central Government within 45 days; one certificate may cover several cosmetics of one manufacturer at one site. New cosmetic needs prior permission COS-3.
6. Validity (Rule 14): perpetual subject to retention fee every 5 years; late fee 2%/month up to 180 days.
7. Changes (Rule 15): change in constitution → fresh registration within 180 days; labelling/composition/testing changes informed within 15 days; name/address changes approved within 60 days. Suspension/cancellation (Rule 16) with appeal in 30 days.
8. Already-registered product imported by another importer: Form COS-4 → import registration number COS-4A (3 years).
9. Labelling: RC number ("RC/RC No./Reg. Cert. No.") and importer's name and address on unit pack; India-specific stickers in bonded warehouse.
10. Customs: declaration of compliance (Rule 19); port officer may sample and detain; defects that cannot be remedied → re-export or destruction within 2 months (Rule 20). Personal-use baggage allowed (Rule 21); only specified ports of entry (Rule 22).
11. Prohibited (Rule 18; section 10): products banned in country of origin; use-before date not more than 6 months beyond import; containing hexachlorophene; tested on animals after 12 November 2014; not of standard quality, misbranded, adulterated or spurious; Central Government may ban any cosmetic in public interest (section 10A).
questions.question: Discuss the regulatory requirements for import of cosmetics into India under the Cosmetics Rules, 2020. Add a note on cosmetics whose import is prohibited.

questions.answer:
1. Misbranded (section 17C): contains a non-prescribed colour; not labelled in the prescribed manner; label/container carries a false or misleading statement.
2. Spurious (17D): made or imported under the name of another cosmetic; imitation or substitute that deceives; label names a fictitious or non-existent manufacturer; substituted wholly/partly; falsely claims to be a particular maker's product.
3. Adulterated (17E): filthy, putrid or decomposed matter; insanitary preparation/storage; container of poisonous or deleterious material; non-prescribed colour; harmful or toxic substance.
4. Prohibitions (section 18): no manufacture for sale, sale, stocking or distribution of cosmetics that are not of standard quality, misbranded, adulterated or spurious, or containing ingredients that make them unsafe; no manufacture without licence (18(c)). Section 26A – Central Government can prohibit harmful cosmetics.
5. Rule 39 specific bans: IS 4707 Part 2 Annex A raw materials; non-permitted colours (Tenth Schedule; colours limited to As 2 ppm, Pb 20 ppm, heavy metals 100 ppm); hexachlorophene except soap ≤ 1% with warning; mercury only 70 ppm in eye products as preservative, ≤ 1 ppm unintentional; lead and arsenic compounds as colours; testing on animals.
6. Penalties (section 27A): spurious or adulterated – imprisonment up to three years and fine; other contraventions – up to one year, or fine, or both. Import contraventions punished under section 13.
7. Confiscation (section 31; Rules 53–54) of stock and, for misbranded/adulterated/unlicensed manufacture, implements, machinery, packages and vehicles; substandard goods destroyed under inspector's supervision.
8. Administrative action: suspension/cancellation of licence or registration after show cause; stop-work orders.
questions.question: What are misbranded, adulterated and spurious cosmetics? Discuss the prohibitions on manufacture and sale of cosmetics and the offences and penalties under the Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940.

questions.answer:
1. Inner and outer label: name of cosmetic; name and full address of manufacturer (actual maker or "Made in…"; small packs ≤ 30 g/60 mL may give name + principal place with PIN); use before/expiry (month and year).
2. Batch number preceded by "B", "Batch No.", "Lot" etc. (not for ≤ 10 g or ≤ 25 mL; soaps show month and year of manufacture).
3. Manufacturing licence number preceded by "M", "M. L. No." or "Mfg. Lic. No.".
4. Outer label: net contents by weight/volume (exempt for perfumes ≤ 60 mL and solids ≤ 30 g).
5. Where a hazard exists: directions for safe use, warnings, names and quantities of hazardous ingredients.
6. Ingredients list headed "INGREDIENTS": those > 1% in descending order, then ≤ 1% in any order (exempt ≤ 60 mL / 30 g).
7. Imported: RC number and importer's name and address; stickering in bonded warehouse.
8. Single label carries all; BIS labelling rules; export labels follow importing country plus core particulars.
questions.question: List the labelling requirements for cosmetics under Rule 34 of the Cosmetics Rules, 2020.

questions.answer:
1. Definition (Rule 3): a licence granted by the SLA to a person who intends to use the manufacturing site of another licensee to manufacture his cosmetic.
2. Licence: application COS-5, licence COS-8, own premises, staff and testing facilities; independent.
3. Loan licence: application COS-6, licence COS-9, uses host's premises, plant, staff and testing; deemed cancelled or suspended if the host's COS-8 is cancelled or suspended.
4. Both: perpetual with retention fee every five years; same conditions of manufacture and testing; separate licence per premises.
5. Users: brand owners, marketing companies, start-ups – low investment, fast entry; responsibility for product quality stays with the loan licensee.
questions.question: What is a loan licence? Compare a licence and a loan licence for cosmetic manufacture.

questions.answer:
1. Hair dyes with p-phenylenediamine or other dyes (Rule 37): caution in English and local languages on inner and outer labels – may irritate skin, do a preliminary test, not for dyeing eyelashes or eyebrows (may cause blindness).
2. Pack insert: skin test – clean small area behind the ear or inner forearm, apply a little prepared dye, let dry, wash after 24 hours; no irritation → no hypersensitivity; repeat before every application.
3. Fluoride toothpaste (Rule 38): fluoride not more than 1000 ppm; fluoride content in ppm on tube and carton; expiry date on tube and carton.
4. Reason: PPD is a strong sensitiser; fluoride is beneficial but excess causes fluorosis in children.
questions.question: Write the special labelling provisions for hair dyes and fluoride toothpastes under the Cosmetics Rules, 2020.

questions.answer:
1. Must comply with BIS standards (Ninth Schedule); if none, with these rules and country-of-origin standards.
2. Raw materials in Annex A of IS 4707 (Part 2) must not be added.
3. Only colours permitted by IS 4707 and the Tenth Schedule; permitted organic colours ≤ 2 ppm arsenic (as As2O3), ≤ 20 ppm lead, ≤ 100 ppm other heavy metals.
4. No hexachlorophene, except soaps ≤ 1% w/w with "Contains hexachlorophene – not to be used on babies".
5. Mercury: ≤ 70 ppm (0.007%) as preservative in eye-area products; ≤ 1 ppm unintentional in others.
6. Lead and arsenic compounds banned as colourants.
7. No person shall use any animal for testing cosmetics.
questions.question: State the provisions of Rule 39 of the Cosmetics Rules, 2020 regarding standards and prohibited substances.

questions.answer:
1. New cosmetic: contains a novel ingredient not used anywhere in the world or not recognised for cosmetic use in national/international literature.
2. Apply to the Central Licensing Authority in Form COS-12 with fee and data on safety and effectiveness.
3. If satisfied the product is safe and effective, CLA grants prior permission in Form COS-3 with conditions.
4. COS-3 must accompany the import registration application (COS-1) or manufacturing licence application (COS-5/6); SLA cannot license without it.
5. Safety evaluation tests per IS 4011:2018 (BIS methods of test for safety evaluation of cosmetics); animal testing not allowed, so validated alternatives and human patch tests are used.
questions.question: Describe the procedure and requirements for permission to import or manufacture a new cosmetic.

questions.answer: Import of all cosmetics and permission for new cosmetics: Central Licensing Authority (DCGI, CDSCO). Manufacture, sale and distribution: State Licensing Authority (state drugs controller).
questions.question: Name the authorities responsible for import and for manufacture of cosmetics in India.

questions.answer: COS-2: import registration certificate; COS-8: licence to manufacture cosmetics; COS-9: loan licence to manufacture cosmetics.
questions.question: What are Forms COS-2, COS-8 and COS-9?

questions.answer: A whole-time employee holding a PCI-approved Diploma in Pharmacy, or registered under the Pharmacy Act, 1948, or passed Intermediate with chemistry (or equivalent), or holding a bachelor degree in cosmetic technology (Rule 26).
questions.question: Give the qualifications of the competent technical person for cosmetic manufacture.

questions.answer:
1. Layers: epidermis (stratum basale, spinosum, granulosum, lucidum on palms/soles, corneum), dermis (fibroblasts, collagen, elastin, hyaluronan, vessels, glands, follicles), hypodermis (fat). Diagram.
2. Turnover: basal keratinocytes → corneocytes in about four weeks; desquamation by proteases.
3. Barrier 'bricks and mortar': corneocytes with cornified envelope; intercellular lamellae of ceramides, cholesterol, free fatty acids from lamellar bodies; corneodesmosomes.
4. NMF from filaggrin: amino acids, PCA, urocanic acid, lactate, urea – keeps 10–20% water.
5. Acid mantle pH 4.5–5.5 – barrier enzymes, controlled desquamation, microbiome; TEWL measures barrier.
6. Dry skin: low humidity, harsh surfactants, hot water, ageing, filaggrin defects → loss of lipids and NMF → enzymes inactive → corneocytes stick → scaling, roughness, cracks, itch; cycle of water loss.
7. Acne: pilosebaceous unit; androgens ↑ sebum; follicular hyperkeratinisation → microcomedone → open/closed comedones; C. acnes lipases → FFA, inflammation → papules, pustules, nodules, scars and PIH; aggravated by comedogenic cosmetics and occlusion.
8. Cosmetic link: humectant + occlusive + barrier lipids for dry skin; oil control, salicylic acid, niacinamide, non-comedogenic vehicles for acne.
questions.question: Describe the structure of the skin with emphasis on the stratum corneum barrier. Explain how this structure relates to dry skin and acne.

questions.answer:
1. Follicle: bulb with matrix cells and dermal papilla, melanocytes, sebaceous gland, arrector pili.
2. Shaft: cuticle (6–10 overlapping scales, lipid layer; shine and combability), cortex (keratin macrofibrils, melanin; strength), medulla (core).
3. Chemistry: cystine-rich keratin; disulphide (perms, depilatories, bleach), hydrogen (water setting), salt bonds (pH; IEP about 3.7); negative charge → cationic conditioners bind.
4. Cycle: anagen (2–7 years, 85–90% of hairs), catagen (2–3 weeks), telogen (about 3 months, 10–15%), exogen (shedding); growth ~1 cm/month; ~100 hairs/day normal loss.
5. Problems: androgenetic alopecia (DHT via 5α-reductase miniaturises follicles, shortens anagen); telogen effluvium (shift to telogen after fever, childbirth, stress); dandruff/seborrhoeic dermatitis (Malassezia → irritant fatty acids → flaking); greying (melanocyte loss, oxidative stress); weathering, split ends, frizz from cuticle damage; breakage from chemical treatments.
6. Cosmetic approaches: conditioners, anti-dandruff shampoos, mild cleansing, protection from heat and chemicals.
questions.question: Describe the structure of hair and the hair growth cycle. Discuss common hair and scalp problems.

questions.answer:
1. Melanocytes in basal layer; melanosomes transferred to ~30–40 keratinocytes (epidermal melanin unit).
2. Pathway: tyrosine → DOPA → dopaquinone by tyrosinase; with cysteine → pheomelanin (red-yellow); without → DHI/DHICA → eumelanin (brown-black).
3. Regulation: UV → DNA damage → α-MSH → MC1R → tyrosinase ↑; inflammation, hormones and visible light also stimulate.
4. Disorders: melasma, post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation, solar lentigines, freckles, tan, uneven tone; darker skin types (III–V) prone to PIH and melasma.
5. Cosmeceutical targets: tyrosinase inhibitors, transfer blockers, exfoliation, antioxidants, sunscreen.
6. Ageing: intrinsic (genetic, hormonal; fine wrinkles, thin dry skin) vs extrinsic/photoageing (UV → ROS → MMPs degrade collagen, less synthesis, solar elastosis; coarse wrinkles, spots); glycation stiffens collagen; hyaluronan falls; repeated muscle folding forms expression lines.
7. Approaches: sunscreen, retinoids, antioxidants, peptides, AHAs, moisturisers.
questions.question: Explain melanogenesis and the types of hyperpigmentation. Add a note on skin ageing and wrinkle formation.

questions.answer:
1. Eccrine sweat: watery, mainly wetness; foot odour from bacterial keratin breakdown.
2. Apocrine sweat (armpits, groin; from puberty): lipids, proteins and odour precursors, odourless when fresh.
3. Skin bacteria (Corynebacterium, Staphylococcus) convert precursors into volatile fatty acids (e.g. 3-methyl-2-hexenoic acid), thioalcohols and steroid derivatives → odour.
4. Needs sweat + bacteria + time; occlusion and hair increase it.
5. Control: antiperspirants (aluminium salts reduce sweat), deodorants (antimicrobials, esterase inhibitors like triethyl citrate, low pH), odour absorbers (zinc ricinoleate), fragrance masking, hygiene.
questions.question: Explain the causes of body odour and the strategies to control it.

questions.answer:
1. Plaque: biofilm on acquired pellicle.
2. Caries: S. mutans and lactobacilli ferment sugars; plaque pH below ~5.5 dissolves enamel; saliva and fluoride remineralise.
3. Calculus: mineralised plaque.
4. Gingivitis (bleeding gums): plaque inflammation at gum line, reversible; periodontitis destroys ligament and bone.
5. Halitosis: anaerobes on tongue produce volatile sulphur compounds (H2S, methyl mercaptan).
6. Dentine hypersensitivity: exposed dentine with open tubules; stimuli move tubular fluid (hydrodynamic theory) → sharp pain.
7. Stains, erosion, dry mouth, ulcers.
questions.question: Discuss common problems of the oral cavity relevant to cosmetic oral care products.

questions.answer:
1. Miliaria: blockage of eccrine sweat ducts in hot, humid weather; sweat leaks into skin.
2. Crystallina – block in or under stratum corneum; clear tiny vesicles.
3. Rubra (prickly heat) – deeper in epidermis; itchy, prickling red papules on trunk, neck, folds.
4. Profunda – dermo-epidermal junction; flesh-coloured papules after repeated rubra.
5. Contributing: occlusive clothes and heavy creams, swollen stratum corneum, Staphylococcus slime.
6. Care: keep cool and dry, loose clothing, absorbent cooling powders (talc/starch, zinc oxide, calamine, menthol), avoid occlusive products.
questions.question: What is prickly heat? Describe its types and the care measures.

questions.answer:
1. Face: many sebaceous glands, sun-exposed; mild pH-balanced cleanser removing sebum, pollution and make-up; moisturiser, sunscreen, oil control or anti-ageing as needed.
2. Eyelids: thinnest skin, near eye; non-stinging, ophthalmologist-tested removers (oil or biphasic for waterproof make-up); light eye creams.
3. Lips: no sebaceous glands, thin stratum corneum; occlusive balms with UV protection.
4. Under-arm: apocrine glands, occlusion, friction, shaving; mild wash, deodorant/antiperspirant without irritation.
5. General principles: match surfactant strength to sebum level, maintain acid mantle, protect from sun.
questions.question: Describe the cleansing and care needs of the face, eyelids, lips and under-arm.

questions.answer:
1. Water-soluble hygroscopic molecules inside corneocytes.
2. Formed mainly from breakdown of filaggrin in the upper stratum corneum.
3. Composition: free amino acids (largest part), pyrrolidone carboxylic acid (PCA), urocanic acid, lactate, urea, sugars and salts.
4. Function: binds water, keeps stratum corneum hydrated and flexible, allows desquamation enzymes to work; urocanic acid contributes to acidity.
5. Reduced by harsh washing, ageing, filaggrin mutations → dry skin; replaced cosmetically by sodium PCA, urea, lactate, glycerin.
questions.question: What is natural moisturising factor (NMF)? Give its composition and importance.

questions.answer: Increased sebum production (androgens), follicular hyperkeratinisation, colonisation by Cutibacterium acnes, and inflammation.
questions.question: State the four key factors in the pathogenesis of acne.

questions.answer: Anagen (growth, 2–7 years), catagen (regression, 2–3 weeks), telogen (rest, about 3 months), exogen (shedding).
questions.question: Name the phases of the hair growth cycle with approximate durations.

questions.answer: The slightly acidic surface film (pH about 4.5–5.5) formed from sebum, sweat, free fatty acids and lactic acid; it supports barrier enzymes and friendly skin microbes.
questions.question: What is the acid mantle of skin?

questions.answer:
1. Structure: hydrophilic head + lipophilic tail; CMC, Krafft point.
2. Anionic: soaps, SLS, SLES, ammonium lauryl sulphate, AOS, SCI, sarcosinates, glutamates – cleansing and foaming (shampoo, body wash, toothpaste, syndets); may irritate.
3. Cationic: cetrimonium, behentrimonium chloride, esterquats, benzalkonium, CPC – conditioning, antistatic, antimicrobial.
4. Amphoteric: cocamidopropyl betaine, amphoacetates, sultaines – mild, foam/viscosity boosters, baby shampoos.
5. Non-ionic: fatty alcohol ethoxylates, polysorbates, sorbitan esters, glyceryl stearate, APGs, cocamide MEA – emulsifiers, solubilisers, mild cleansers; may bind preservatives.
6. HLB (Griffin) 0–20: E/5 for ethoxylates; 20(1 − S/A) for esters.
7. Ranges: 3–6 w/o emulsifier; 7–9 wetting; 8–18 o/w; 13–15 detergent; 15–18 solubiliser.
8. Required HLB of the oil phase (e.g. sum of fractions × required HLB of each oil); blend two emulsifiers: HLB(mix) = f·HLB(A) + (1−f)·HLB(B); e.g. Span 80 (4.3) + Tween 80 (15) to reach required HLB.
9. Limitations: HLB ignores temperature (PIT), chemical type and oil polarity; packing parameter predicts micelle shape.
10. Mildness: zein test, mixed micelles reduce irritation.
questions.question: Classify surfactants used in cosmetics with examples and applications. Explain the HLB concept and its use in formulating emulsions.

questions.answer:
1. Need: water, nutrients, repeated use; protect consumer and product; GMP first.
2. Ideal: broad spectrum, low concentration, pH-stable, water-partitioning, compatible, non-irritant, regulated, cheap.
3. Parabens: broad, pH 3–8, cheap, well studied; bound by non-ionics, public concern, some banned (EU).
4. Phenoxyethanol: stable, compatible; weak alone → boosters.
5. Organic acids (benzoic, sorbic, dehydroacetic): mild, natural-accepted; active only undissociated at low pH.
6. Formaldehyde releasers: effective vs bacteria, cheap; sensitisation, labelling.
7. Isothiazolinones: active at ppm; high allergy, restricted to rinse-off (EU).
8. Quats, benzyl alcohol, multifunctional glycols/esters – roles and limits.
9. Factors: pH vs pKa; oil:water partition; micellar binding by non-ionics; interactions with proteins, powders, anionics; packaging sorption and design; water activity; temperature/time; microbial load and GMP; product structure; synergy with EDTA and glycols (hurdle approach).
10. Challenge test (ISO 11930): inoculate separately P. aeruginosa, S. aureus, E. coli, C. albicans, A. brasiliensis; count at intervals up to 28 days; compare log reductions with criteria; fail → reformulate or improve packaging.
questions.question: Classify antimicrobial preservatives used in cosmetics with their merits and demerits. Discuss factors affecting preservative efficacy and the challenge test.

questions.answer:
1. Vanishing cream (o/w): stearic acid 15–25% (oil phase, film), alkali (KOH/NaOH/TEA) neutralises about 15–25% to form soap emulsifier in situ, glycerin/sorbitol humectant 5–10%, cetyl alcohol, preservative, perfume, water to 100.
2. Method: melt stearic acid ~75 °C; dissolve alkali + humectant in water at same temperature; add water phase to oil with stirring; cool with slow stirring; perfume below 40 °C; age for pearlescence.
3. Properties: spreads and 'vanishes', matt non-greasy film, pearly lustre from stearic acid crystals; day cream/foundation base.
4. Cold cream (w/o): white beeswax 10–20%, mineral oil/almond oil 40–55%, borax 0.5–1% (reacts with cerotic acid to form sodium cerotate emulsifier), water/rose water 20–35%, preservative, antioxidant, perfume.
5. Method: melt wax and oil ~70 °C; dissolve borax in hot water; add water slowly to oil phase with stirring; cool; perfume.
6. Properties: cooling sensation from evaporating water; cleansing, massage, night cream; may invert to o/w with more water.
7. Comparison: type o/w vs w/o; greasy feel low vs high; use day vs cleansing/night; emulsifier stearate soap vs sodium cerotate; washability easy vs harder.
questions.question: Give the building blocks (formula with functions) and method of preparation of a vanishing cream and a cold cream. Compare the two.

questions.answer:
1. Primary surfactant: SLES, ALS, AOS, SCI – cleansing, foam (8–15% active).
2. Secondary: cocamidopropyl betaine, cocamide MEA, APGs – mildness, foam, viscosity.
3. Conditioning: polyquaternium-10, guar hydroxypropyltrimonium chloride, dimethicone, panthenol – coacervate deposition.
4. Thickener: NaCl (salt curve), PEG-150 distearate, acrylates.
5. Pearliser: glycol distearate.
6. Actives: zinc pyrithione, piroctone olamine (anti-dandruff), suspended by polymers.
7. pH adjuster (citric acid, pH 5–6.5), chelator (EDTA), preservative, perfume, colour, water.
questions.question: Write the building blocks of a shampoo with functions of each.

questions.answer:
1. Abrasive 20–50%: calcium carbonate, dicalcium phosphate, hydrated silica – cleaning, stain removal; controlled abrasivity.
2. Humectant 20–40%: sorbitol, glycerin – prevents drying.
3. Binder 0.5–2%: sodium CMC, xanthan, carrageenan, thickening silica.
4. Foaming agent 1–2%: SLS.
5. Active: NaF or sodium monofluorophosphate (≤ 1000 ppm fluoride in India); potassium nitrate; zinc citrate.
6. Sweetener (saccharin), flavour (peppermint, menthol), preservative, colour, water.
7. Compatibility: calcium carbonate binds NaF → use MFP; silica compatible with NaF.
questions.question: Give the composition of a toothpaste with the function of each ingredient.

questions.answer:
1. Soap: sodium salts of fatty acids by saponification (tallow/palm + coconut ~80:20); syndet: mainly sodium cocoyl isethionate with stearic acid, fillers, emollients; combars mix both.
2. pH: soap 9–10; syndet 5.5–7.
3. Hard water: soap forms scum; syndet does not.
4. Barrier: soap removes lipids and swells stratum corneum, raises TEWL; syndet milder.
5. Lather: soap good; syndet creamy.
6. Quality: soap graded by TFM (BIS Grade 1 ≥ 76%, 2 ≥ 70%, 3 ≥ 60%).
7. Cost: soap low; syndet higher; syndet preferred for dry, sensitive, acne-prone, atopic skin and babies.
questions.question: Compare soaps and syndet bars.

questions.answer:
1. By origin: natural (essential oils, absolutes, resinoids), animal (now synthetic replacements), synthetic aroma chemicals.
2. By family: floral, fresh (citrus, green, aquatic), oriental/amber, woody, chypre, fougère, gourmand.
3. By concentration: parfum ~20–30%, EDP ~15–20%, EDT ~5–15%, cologne ~2–5%, mist ~1–3%.
4. By notes: top, heart, base (fixatives).
5. EU Regulation 1223/2009 Annex III: 26 allergens labelled above 0.001% leave-on / 0.01% rinse-off – e.g. limonene, linalool, citral, citronellol, geraniol, eugenol, isoeugenol, coumarin, cinnamal, benzyl alcohol, benzyl benzoate, benzyl salicylate, hexyl cinnamal, farnesol, oakmoss and treemoss extracts.
6. HICC, atranol, chloroatranol, lilial now banned; Regulation 2023/1545 extends labelling to about 80 allergens.
questions.question: Classify perfumes. Name the fragrance allergens requiring labelling under EU regulation.

questions.answer:
1. Parabens: weak oestrogenic activity in vitro, rising with chain length; 2004 tumour-tissue study showed presence, not causation. EU: methyl/ethyl ≤ 0.4% single, 0.8% mixtures; propyl + butyl ≤ 0.14% total and not in leave-on nappy-area products for under-3s; isopropyl, isobutyl, phenyl, benzyl, pentyl parabens banned. Short-chain parabens are low sensitisers; replacements may be worse.
2. Formaldehyde liberators: DMDM hydantoin, imidazolidinyl/diazolidinyl urea, quaternium-15, bronopol; formaldehyde is a sensitiser and carcinogen (EU 1B); EU label "releases formaldehyde" if released total > 0.001% (Reg. 2022/1181); bronopol can form nitrosamines; heated keratin treatments release gas.
3. 1,4-Dioxane: impurity from ethoxylation (SLES, PEGs, polysorbates); possible carcinogen; prohibited as an ingredient in EU; controlled by vacuum stripping, specifications, GC–MS testing, non-ethoxylated alternatives.
4. Approach: hazard vs risk, margin of safety.
questions.question: Discuss parabens, formaldehyde liberators and 1,4-dioxane as controversial ingredients.

questions.answer:
1. Emollients: hydrocarbons (mineral oil, petrolatum, squalane); triglycerides (almond, coconut, shea butter, caprylic/capric triglyceride); synthetic esters (IPM, IPP, C12–15 alkyl benzoate); fatty alcohols/acids (cetyl, stearyl, stearic acid); silicones (dimethicone); lanolin; waxes; skin-identical lipids (ceramides).
2. By feel: fast-spreading → slow and rich; emollient cascade.
3. Rheology modifiers: natural gums (xanthan, guar, carrageenan); cellulose derivatives (Na CMC, HEC, HPMC); synthetic (carbomers – neutralise, acrylates crosspolymers); associative thickeners (PEG-150 distearate); electrolytes (NaCl in shampoos); clays and silica (bentonite, MAS); lipid structurants (fatty alcohols, waxes).
4. Desired flow: shear-thinning with yield value for suspension and easy spreading; thixotropy for gels.
questions.question: Classify emollients and rheology modifiers used in cosmetics with examples.

questions.answer: A preservative efficacy test in which the product is inoculated with Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Staphylococcus aureus, Escherichia coli, Candida albicans and Aspergillus brasiliensis and counts are followed for 28 days against log-reduction criteria (ISO 11930).
questions.question: What is the challenge test? Name the test organisms.

questions.answer: Only part of the stearic acid is neutralised to soap; the remaining free stearic acid crystallises as fine plate-like crystals that reflect light, giving a pearly sheen after ageing.
questions.question: Why does a vanishing cream show a pearly lustre?

questions.answer: It is not added deliberately; it is a by-product of ethoxylation and remains as a trace impurity in ethoxylated ingredients such as SLES, PEGs and polysorbates.
questions.question: What is the origin of 1,4-dioxane in cosmetics?

questions.answer:
1. UV bands: UVB 290–320 nm (burn, DNA damage), UVA2 320–340, UVA1 340–400 nm (photoageing, pigmentation); visible light worsens melasma.
2. Mechanism: organic absorbers vs inorganic ZnO/TiO2 (absorb and scatter; coated; micronised/nano).
3. Chemical classes: PABA esters, cinnamates (octinoxate), salicylates (octisalate, homosalate), octocrylene, ensulizole (UVB); benzophenones (oxybenzone), avobenzone (UVA1, photounstable), anthranilates; newer broad-spectrum triazines and benzotriazoles (bemotrizinol, bisoctrizole), ecamsule.
4. SPF = MED protected/MED unprotected at 2 mg/cm² (ISO 24444); SPF 15/30/50 ≈ 93/97/98% UVB blocked.
5. UVA: UVA-PF by PPD in vivo or ISO 24443 in vitro; critical wavelength ≥ 370 nm = broad spectrum; Japanese PA+ to PA++++ (PPD 2, 4, 8, 16).
6. Water resistance 40/80 min; in vitro Mansur method for screening.
7. Regulation: India – cosmetic under Cosmetics Rules 2020, permitted ingredients, truthful claims, import registration; EU – cosmetic, Annex VI filters with limits, Recommendation 2006/647/EC (UVA-PF ≥ ⅓ SPF, λc 370 nm, bands low 6–10, medium 15–25, high 30–50, very high 50+, no 'sunblock'); USA – OTC drug monograph, broad-spectrum test, 2019 proposal: only ZnO and TiO2 GRASE; Australia – TGA therapeutic goods; Japan – PA.
8. Design: combine filters, photostabilise avobenzone, film formers, solvent emollients, coated minerals, tinting for dark skin, test and label reapplication.
questions.question: Classify sunscreens with examples. Explain SPF, UVA protection measurement and the regulatory aspects of sunscreens.

questions.answer:
1. Approach: biology → active at permitted level → vehicle → stability → safety → proof; avoid drug claims (hydroquinone, tretinoin are drugs).
2. Pigmentation biology: tyrosinase pathway, melanosome transfer, UV/visible light, inflammation.
3. Actives: tyrosinase inhibitors – kojic acid, arbutin/alpha-arbutin, licorice (glabridin), azelaic acid, 4-butylresorcinol, vitamin C; transfer blockers – niacinamide, soy; anti-inflammatory/antioxidant – tranexamic acid, vitamin E, ferulic acid; exfoliants – AHAs, retinol; prevention – broad-spectrum sunscreen + iron oxides.
4. Stability: L-ascorbic acid at pH ~3–3.5, oxidises → derivatives (MAP, ascorbyl glucoside, ethyl ascorbic acid), airless/opaque packs; kojic acid colour change.
5. Wrinkle biology: intrinsic and photoageing, MMPs, collagen loss, glycation, hyaluronan loss.
6. Actives: retinol/retinaldehyde/retinyl esters; vitamin C, E, ferulic acid, green tea, CoQ10; peptides (palmitoyl pentapeptide-4, copper tripeptide-1, acetyl hexapeptide-8); AHAs/PHAs; hyaluronic acid; daily sunscreen.
7. Vehicle and delivery: serums, light emulsions; encapsulation (liposomes, NLCs) for retinol; night use; gradual introduction to limit irritation.
8. Evaluation: chromameter/Mexameter, ITA, imaging for tone; profilometry, cutometer, expert grading for wrinkles; irritation and phototoxicity safety.
questions.question: Discuss the design of cosmeceutical formulations for (a) pigmentation and (b) wrinkles.

questions.answer:
1. Legal basis: India Rule 39(7) bans animal testing; import ban for products tested after 12 Nov 2014; EU testing and marketing bans.
2. Safety assessment: ingredient hazard data + exposure (amount, frequency, leave-on/rinse-off, absorption) → SED; MoS = NOAEL/SED ≥ 100; product safety report.
3. Alternatives: skin irritation RhE (OECD 439), corrosion (431), eye – BCOP (437), RhCE (492), HET-CAM; sensitisation – DPRA (442C), KeratinoSens (442D), h-CLAT (442E) in defined approaches; phototoxicity 3T3 NRU (432); genotoxicity Ames, micronucleus; skin absorption Franz cells (428).
4. Human tests on finished products: patch tests, HRIPT, use tests, ophthalmological and non-comedogenicity tests; IS 4011:2018 methods.
5. Stability: real-time, accelerated (40 °C/75% RH), freeze–thaw, centrifuge, light; physical, chemical, packaging checks.
6. Microbiology: limits and challenge test (ISO 11930).
7. Efficacy: corneometer, TEWL, sebumeter, cutometer, chromameter/Mexameter, profilometry, SPF/UVA tests, combing force, plaque/gingival indices; controlled, blinded, statistical design.
8. Claims truthful (Rule 36), ASCI code.

# Unit 1: Cosmetics — Indian regulatory provisions

A formulation scientist who designs a cream, shampoo or toothpaste in India must know, before the first batch is made, whether the product is a cosmetic or a drug, who licenses it, what must appear on the label and which ingredients are forbidden. This unit covers the law that answers those questions: the **Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940** (the Act) and the **Cosmetics Rules, 2020** (the Rules) made under it. The B.Pharm course (BP809ET) gave an outline; here the provisions are studied rule by rule, as an M.Pharm examiner expects.

> Rule numbers below follow the Cosmetics Rules, 2020 as notified (G.S.R. 763(E), 15 December 2020). The Rules have been amended since (for example in 2025). Always read the current consolidated text before applying them in practice.

## 1.1 The legal framework

```text
Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940  (Parliament)
   │  Chapter III  – import of drugs and cosmetics
   │  Chapter IV   – manufacture, sale and distribution of drugs and cosmetics
   │
   ├── Drugs Rules, 1945            (drugs; earlier also cosmetics)
   └── Cosmetics Rules, 2020        (all cosmetic matters from 15 Dec 2020)
          ├─ standards → Bureau of Indian Standards (BIS) Indian Standards (Ninth Schedule)
          ├─ GMP and premises → Seventh Schedule
          └─ permitted colours → Tenth Schedule
```

**History in brief.** Until December 2020, cosmetics were controlled through parts of the Drugs and Cosmetics Rules, 1945: manufacturing licences were issued in **Form 32**, factory premises followed **Schedule M-II**, and BIS standards were listed in **Schedule S**. The Cosmetics Rules, 2020 moved everything into one separate set of rules with its own "COS" forms. Licences granted under the old rules stayed valid until they expired, and holders had to convert them to the new form.

**Authorities (Rule 4).**

| Authority | Who | Responsible for |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Central Licensing Authority (CLA) | Drugs Controller General of India, Central Drugs Standard Control Organisation (CDSCO) | Import of all categories of cosmetics (registration), permission for new cosmetics, coordination with states |
| State Licensing Authority (SLA) | State drugs controller (by whatever name called) | Licences to manufacture for sale or distribution; control of sale, stock and distribution; approval of testing laboratories |
| Inspectors | Appointed by Central or State Government under section 21 of the Act | Inspection of premises, sampling, seizure |
| Government Analyst | Appointed under section 20 of the Act | Testing samples drawn by inspectors |
| Central Cosmetics Laboratory | Notified by the Central Government | Testing and analysis of cosmetics, including import samples and samples sent by courts |

**Standards body.** The Bureau of Indian Standards (BIS) writes the product standards (for example for toothpaste, skin creams, shampoos, soaps, hair dyes). Two BIS standards matter for every formulator:

- **IS 4707 (Part 1)** – dyes, colours and pigments permitted in cosmetics.
- **IS 4707 (Part 2)** – raw materials; its **Annex A** lists materials that must not be added to cosmetics, and other parts give restricted ingredients with limits.
- **IS 4011:2018** – methods of test for safety evaluation of cosmetics (named in the Rules for new cosmetics).

## 1.2 Definition of a cosmetic

**Section 3(aaa) of the Act** defines a cosmetic as any article intended to be **rubbed, poured, sprinkled or sprayed on, or introduced into, or otherwise applied to, the human body or any part of it for cleansing, beautifying, promoting attractiveness, or altering the appearance**, and includes any article intended for use as a **component** of a cosmetic.

Points examiners look for:

1. **Four methods of application** (rubbed, poured, sprinkled, sprayed) plus "introduced into" and "otherwise applied" – so oral products such as toothpaste and mouthwash are covered.
2. **Four purposes** – cleansing, beautifying, promoting attractiveness, altering appearance.
3. **Human body only** – a dog shampoo or a room freshener is not a cosmetic under these Rules.
4. **Components** – raw materials sold for making cosmetics are cosmetics in law.
5. **Intended use decides status** – the same chemical may be a drug or a cosmetic depending on purpose and claims. A product that claims to treat, cure, mitigate or prevent disease, or to affect structure or function of the body, falls within the definition of a **drug** (section 3(b)) and needs drug licensing.

**Other definitions in Rule 3 worth learning**

| Term | Meaning (in plain words) |
| --- | --- |
| New cosmetic | Contains a **novel ingredient** not used anywhere in the world, or not recognised for cosmetic use in any national or international literature |
| Loan licence | A licence that lets a person manufacture his cosmetic at **another licensee's manufacturing site** |
| Use before / date of expiry | The date up to which the cosmetic keeps its characteristics as per standards when stored as stated on the label |
| Import registration certificate | Certificate issued by the CLA (Rule 13) registering a cosmetic for import |
| Legal manufacturer / brand owner | The person who authorises another manufacturer (in India or abroad) to make the cosmetic for him |

**Where do cosmeceuticals stand?** "Cosmeceutical" is a marketing and scientific term, **not a legal category** in India. A cosmeceutical with cosmetic claims (smoother-looking skin, more even-looking tone) is a cosmetic; the moment it claims to treat acne, melasma or alopecia it becomes a drug. India has no "quasi-drug" class like Japan, and no "cosmetic–drug" class like the USA. Ayurvedic and herbal products with medicinal claims are handled under the Ayurveda, Siddha and Unani drug provisions of the Act, not the Cosmetics Rules.

## 1.3 Structure of the Cosmetics Rules, 2020

| Chapter | Content | Key rules |
| --- | --- | --- |
| I | Short title, definitions | 1–3 |
| II | Authorities, officers and laboratory | 4–11 |
| III | Import and registration | 12–22 |
| IV | Manufacture for sale or distribution | 23–31 |
| V | Permission for import or manufacture of new cosmetic | 32 |
| VI | Labelling, packing and standards | 33–39 |
| VII | Sampling, seizure, test reports, confiscation | 40–54 |
| VIII | Approval of laboratories for testing cosmetics | 55 onwards |

Schedules referred to in this unit: **Second** (documents for import and manufacture applications), **Third** (fees), **Seventh** (GMP, premises, plant and equipment), **Eighth** (batch manufacturing records), **Ninth** (BIS standards), **Tenth** (permitted colours).

## 1.4 Regulatory requirements for labelling (Rules 33–39)

**Rule 33** forbids sale or distribution of any cosmetic of Indian origin unless it is made by a **licensed manufacturer** and **labelled and packed** as the Rules require.

**Rule 34 – manner of labelling.**

| Item | Where | Details |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Name of the cosmetic | Inner and outer label | – |
| Name and complete address of the manufacturer (premises where made) | Inner and outer label | If made in a factory not owned by the manufacturer, name and address of the actual manufacturer, or "Made in (country)". For very small packs (30 g or less of solid/semi-solid, 60 mL or less of liquid), the name and principal place of manufacture with PIN code is enough |
| Use before / date of expiry (month and year) | Inner and outer label | Any of the accepted wordings: use before, use by, expiry date, "expiry XX months from manufacture" |
| Batch number | Inner or outer label | Preceded by "B", "Batch No.", "B. No.", "Batch", "Lot No." or "Lot". Not needed for packs of 10 g or less (solid/semi-solid) or 25 mL or less (liquid). Soaps show month and year of manufacture instead |
| Manufacturing licence number | Inner or outer label | Preceded by "M", "M. L. No." or "Mfg. Lic. No." (may be omitted on imported products if the country of origin does not require it) |
| Net contents | Outer label | Weight for solids, fluid measure for liquids, either for semi-solids, plus count if subdivided. Not needed for perfumes/toilet waters of 60 mL or less or solids/semi-solids of 30 g or less |
| Hazard information | Inner label, where a hazard exists | Directions for safe use; warnings and cautions; names and quantities of hazardous or poisonous ingredients |
| Ingredients | Label | Headed "INGREDIENTS"; those above 1% in **descending order** of weight or volume at the time of addition, then those at 1% or less in any order. Not needed for packs of 60 mL or less (liquid) or 30 g or less (solid/semi-solid) |
| Imported cosmetics | Unit pack | Import registration certificate number preceded by "RC", "RC No" or "Reg. Cert. No", with name and address of the importer / registration holder. India-specific labels may be stickered on in the **bonded warehouse** |

Other labelling points:

- If the pack has only **one label**, it must carry everything required on inner and outer labels (Rule 34(6)).
- Labels must also meet any labelling requirement in the relevant **BIS standard** (Rule 34(8)).
- **Export packs** follow the importing country's law but must still show name, batch/lot, use-before date (if any), manufacturer's name and address, and licence number; a code number approved by the SLA may replace the manufacturer's name if the buyer wants (Rule 34(10)).
- **Rule 35** – no one may alter, obliterate or deface the manufacturer's inscriptions on the container, label or wrapper (except with CLA permission).
- **Rule 36** – no cosmetic may make a **false or misleading claim**.
- **Rule 37 – hair dyes** containing p-phenylenediamine or other dyes must carry a **caution** in English and local languages on inner and outer labels: the product may irritate skin, a **preliminary (patch) test** must be done as directed, and it must not be used to dye **eyelashes or eyebrows** because it may cause blindness. The pack must include instructions for the skin test (apply behind the ear or on the inner forearm, leave 24 hours, look for irritation; repeat before every use).
- **Rule 38 – fluoride toothpaste**: fluoride not more than **1000 ppm**, the content in ppm stated on tube and carton, and the expiry date on both.
- **Rule 39(4) – hexachlorophene** in soap (only up to 1%) requires the warning "Contains hexachlorophene – not to be used on babies".

Packaged cosmetics are also subject to the Legal Metrology (Packaged Commodities) Rules, 2011 for net quantity, maximum retail price and consumer care details.

## 1.5 Regulatory provisions relating to import (Chapter III of the Act; Rules 12–22)

**Registration is compulsory (Rule 12).** No cosmetic may be imported unless it is registered by the CLA.

```text
Applicant (foreign manufacturer itself, its authorised Indian agent,
           the importer, or its Indian subsidiary)
      │  Form COS-1 on the online portal + documents (Second Schedule, Part I)
      │  + fee per category per manufacturing site (Third/Fourth Schedule)
      ▼
Central Licensing Authority  ── may require testing at an approved laboratory
      │                         (Fifth Schedule products) and inspection of the
      │                         foreign site at the applicant's cost
      ▼
Import registration certificate – Form COS-2   (decision within 6 months;
                                                appeal to Central Government
                                                within 45 days of rejection)
```

Key provisions:

1. **Authorisation** from the foreign manufacturer to the Indian agent must be authenticated (before a first-class magistrate in India, or the competent authority of the exporting country).
2. One application and one certificate may cover **several cosmetics of the same manufacturer** made at one factory (or factories working as one unit) (Rule 13(4)).
3. **Bulk finished formulation** imported for filling in India needs, in addition, a valid Indian manufacturing licence for filling and details of the brand owner.
4. **New cosmetic** – prior permission in **Form COS-3** (Chapter V) is needed before registration.
5. **Validity (Rule 14)** – the certificate is **valid in perpetuity**, provided a **retention fee** is paid before every five-year period ends. Late payment attracts a late fee of 2% of the retention fee per month for up to 180 days; after that the certificate is deemed cancelled.
6. **Changes (Rule 15)** – a change of constitution needs a fresh registration within 180 days; changes in labelling, composition, testing or specifications must be reported within 15 days with an undertaking of compliance with BIS standards; a change of name or address needs prior approval within 60 days.
7. **Suspension/cancellation (Rule 16)** after show-cause; appeal to the Central Government within 30 days.
8. **Already registered products (Rule 17)** – any other person may import a cosmetic already registered, by applying in **Form COS-4**; an **import registration number** is issued in **Form COS-4A**, valid for **three years**.
9. **Declaration to Customs (Rule 19)** – that the consignment complies with Chapter III of the Act.
10. **Port procedure (Rule 20)** – the port officer may sample a consignment; it can be detained until the Central Cosmetics Laboratory reports. If a defect cannot be remedied, the importer must re-export the goods or hand them over for destruction within two months; a representation may be made within 30 days.
11. **Personal use (Rule 21)** – small quantities in a passenger's baggage, for bona fide personal use, may be imported.
12. **Ports of entry (Rule 22)** – only through the points of entry specified in the Drugs Rules, 1945.

**Prohibition of import of certain cosmetics (Rule 18):**

- a cosmetic whose manufacture, sale or distribution is **prohibited in its country of origin**;
- a cosmetic whose **use-before date is six months or less** from the date of import;
- any cosmetic containing **hexachlorophene**;
- any cosmetic **tested on animals after 12 November 2014**.

**Section 10 of the Act** also prohibits import of cosmetics that are **not of standard quality, misbranded, adulterated or spurious**, and cosmetics containing ingredients that may make them unsafe or harmful; **Section 10A** lets the Central Government prohibit the import of any cosmetic in the public interest.

## 1.6 Misbranded, adulterated and spurious cosmetics

These three terms are defined in Chapter IV of the Act (with matching provisions for imports in Chapter III).

| Term (section) | A cosmetic is deemed to be this if … |
| --- | --- |
| **Misbranded (17C)** | it contains a **colour not prescribed**; or it is **not labelled in the prescribed manner**; or its label or container bears a statement that is **false or misleading** in any particular |
| **Spurious (17D)** | it is made or imported under a **name that belongs to another cosmetic**; or it is an **imitation of, or substitute for**, another cosmetic, or resembles it so as to deceive; or its label names a **fictitious or non-existent** manufacturer; or it has been **substituted** wholly or partly by another cosmetic; or it falsely purports to be the product of a manufacturer of whom it is not |
| **Adulterated (17E)** | it contains **filthy, putrid or decomposed** substance; it was prepared, packed or stored under **insanitary conditions** so it may be contaminated or injurious; its **container** is made of a poisonous or harmful substance; it contains a **non-prescribed colour** for colouring; or it contains a **harmful or toxic substance** that may make it injurious to health |

Memory aid: **misbranded = wrong label**, **spurious = wrong identity**, **adulterated = wrong contents or conditions**.

## 1.7 Regulatory provisions relating to manufacture (Chapter IV of the Rules)

### Conditions for obtaining a licence (Rules 23–31)

```text
Applicant ──► Form COS-5 (licence) or COS-6 (loan licence), online
              + fee (Third Schedule) + documents (Second Schedule, Part II)
              + Form COS-7: self-declaration of GMP, premises, plant and
                equipment as per the Seventh Schedule
              + COS-3 permission from CLA if it is a new cosmetic
                    │
                    ▼
State Licensing Authority: scrutiny → licence within 45 days
   Form COS-8 (licence) / Form COS-9 (loan licence)
                    │
                    ▼
Licence uploaded on the CDSCO website → manufacture may begin
                    │
                    ▼
SLA inspects within 30 days to verify COS-7
 (if not inspected in time, the licence is deemed valid; false
  self-declaration → show cause → cancellation, or stop-work order
  until deficiencies are corrected)
```

- **Separate licence for each premises** (Rule 24).
- **Rejection** – reasons and the inspection report are given; a further application with fee within six months may be considered (Rule 28); appeal to the State Government within 90 days (Rule 29).
- **Validity (Rule 30)** – COS-8 and COS-9 are **valid in perpetuity** subject to a **retention fee** before each five-year period ends (same 2% per month late fee up to 180 days, then deemed cancellation).
- **Inspection (Rule 31)** – licensed premises are inspected at least **once in three years**, or as needed on a **risk-based approach**.

### Conditions of the licence (Rule 26)

1. **Competent technical staff** – manufacture under the direction and personal supervision of at least **one whole-time employee** who holds a **Diploma in Pharmacy** approved by PCI, or is a **registered pharmacist**, or has passed the **Intermediate examination with chemistry** (or equivalent), or holds a **bachelor degree in cosmetic technology**.
2. **Premises** complying with the **Seventh Schedule** (GMP, premises, plant and equipment).
3. **Testing** – either the manufacturer's own staff, premises and laboratory equipment for testing raw materials and products, or an arrangement with a laboratory **approved by the CLA and accredited by NABL**. Each batch of raw material and each batch of finished product must be tested; test records kept for **three years** from manufacture.
4. **Batch records** as in the **Eighth Schedule**, kept for **three years after the batch's expiry**.
5. **Inspectors** may enter with or without notice, inspect and take samples (receipt in **Form COS-10**); an **inspection book (Form COS-11)** is kept for the inspector's remarks.
6. **Changes** in labelling, composition, testing, specification or documentation must be reported to the SLA within **30 days** with an undertaking of compliance with BIS standards.
7. **Change in constitution** of the firm – the existing licence remains valid for at most **six months**, by which time a fresh licence is needed; change of name or address needs approval within 60 days.
8. **Soap** makers are exempt from the testing and documentary clauses; their testing procedure is as approved by the SLA.

### Loan licence

A **loan licence** allows a person who has **no manufacturing facility of his own** (often a brand owner) to manufacture his cosmetic at the **licensed premises of another manufacturer**, using that site's plant, staff and testing set-up, but under his own name and responsibility.

| Point | Licence | Loan licence |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Application form | COS-5 | COS-6 |
| Licence form | COS-8 | COS-9 |
| Own premises | Required | Uses another licensee's premises |
| Dependence | Independent | A COS-9 is **deemed cancelled or suspended** if the host site's COS-8 is cancelled or suspended |
| Typical user | Factory owner | Brand owner, marketing company, start-up |

Advantages: low investment, fast market entry, use of established GMP facilities. Responsibilities: the loan licensee is answerable for the quality of his product; the host must have capacity and the right product category.

### Permission for new cosmetics (Rule 32)

Anyone intending to import or manufacture a **new cosmetic** applies to the CLA in **Form COS-12** with fees and **data on safety and effectiveness**. If satisfied, the CLA grants prior permission in **Form COS-3**, which is then attached to the import or manufacture application. Safety evaluation tests must follow **IS 4011:2018**.

## 1.8 Prohibition of manufacture and sale of certain cosmetics

**Section 18 of the Act** forbids anyone to manufacture for sale, sell, stock, exhibit or distribute any cosmetic that is **not of standard quality, misbranded, adulterated or spurious**, or that contains any ingredient which may make it unsafe or harmful under ordinary conditions of use, or to manufacture any cosmetic **without a licence** (section 18(c)). **Section 26A** allows the Central Government to prohibit or restrict the manufacture, sale or distribution of a cosmetic that is harmful, in the public interest.

**Rule 39 – standards and specific prohibitions:**

| Provision | Requirement |
| --- | --- |
| 39(1) | Must comply with the BIS standard (Ninth Schedule). If no Indian standard exists, it must meet these Rules and the standards of its country of origin |
| 39(2) | Raw materials in **Annex A of IS 4707 (Part 2)** must not be added |
| 39(3) | Only dyes, colours and pigments permitted by IS 4707 (Parts 1/2) and the **Tenth Schedule**. Permitted synthetic and natural organic colours may contain not more than **2 ppm arsenic** (as As2O3), **20 ppm lead** and **100 ppm** of other heavy metals in total |
| 39(4) | **Hexachlorophene** not to be used, except in soaps up to **1% w/w** with the warning label |
| 39(5) | **Mercury**: eye-area products may contain up to **70 ppm (0.007%)** as a preservative; in all other products, unintentional mercury must not exceed **1 ppm** |
| 39(6) | **Lead and arsenic compounds** must not be used for colouring cosmetics |
| 39(7) | **No person shall use any animal for testing of cosmetics** |

India banned animal testing of cosmetics in 2014 and, as noted above, also bans import of cosmetics tested on animals after 12 November 2014. Safety therefore rests on ingredient data, human-safe testing and validated alternative methods (see Unit 4).

## 1.9 Sampling, testing and offences and penalties

**Sampling and testing (Chapter VII).**

- A **purchaser** may get a cosmetic tested by a Government Analyst (application in **Form COS-13**, report in **Form COS-14**) under section 26 of the Act.
- **Inspectors** draw samples (intimation **Form COS-10**), may order stock not to be disposed of (**Form COS-18**), seize stock and records (**Form COS-15**), and send sealed samples to the Government Analyst (memorandum **Form COS-17**); the analyst reports in **Form COS-19** with test protocols.
- Courts may send samples to the Central Cosmetics Laboratory (Forms COS-20 and COS-21).

**Offences and penalties.**

| Offence | Provision | Punishment (outline) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Manufacture for sale, sale, stock or exhibition of a **spurious or adulterated** cosmetic | Section 27A(i) | Imprisonment up to **three years** and fine |
| Any other contravention of Chapter IV or the rules for cosmetics (misbranded cosmetic, sale without licence, labelling breaches, etc.) | Section 27A(ii) | Imprisonment up to **one year**, or fine, or both |
| Import in contravention of Chapter III | Section 13 | Imprisonment and/or fine, graded by the type of contravention; the goods are liable to confiscation |
| After conviction | Section 31 and Rules 53–54 | **Confiscation** of the stock; for misbranded (17C) or adulterated (17E) cosmetics, or manufacture without licence (18(c)), also the implements, machinery, packages and vehicles used. The court refers confiscated goods to the inspector; substandard goods are destroyed under supervision |

Repeat offenders face heavier punishment under the Act. Exact fine amounts have been revised by amendments over the years, so quote them only from the current text.

**Other administrative actions:** suspension or cancellation of import registration or licence after a show-cause notice; stop-work orders; recall of batches.

## 1.10 India and the European Union compared

| Point | India | European Union |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Law | D&C Act, 1940 + Cosmetics Rules, 2020 | Regulation (EC) No 1223/2009 |
| Pre-market step | Import registration (COS-2) or state manufacturing licence (COS-8/9) | Safety assessment report, a named responsible person, notification on the EU portal |
| Ingredient lists | BIS IS 4707 (prohibited Annex A, permitted colours), Tenth Schedule | Annexes II (prohibited), III (restricted), IV (colourants), V (preservatives), VI (UV filters) |
| Animal testing | Banned (testing, and import of products tested after Nov 2014) | Banned for products and ingredients, with a marketing ban |
| Claims | No false or misleading claims; disease claims make it a drug | Claims must meet common criteria and be substantiated |

## Remember

- Cosmetic: section 3(aaa) – rubbed, poured, sprinkled, sprayed, introduced or applied to the human body for cleansing, beautifying, promoting attractiveness, altering appearance; includes components.
- Cosmetics Rules, 2020: G.S.R. 763(E), 15 December 2020; CLA (CDSCO) for import and new cosmetics, SLA for manufacture and sale.
- Import: COS-1 → COS-2 (perpetual, retention fee every 5 years); new cosmetic COS-12 → COS-3; already registered product COS-4 → COS-4A (3 years).
- Import bans: banned in country of origin, shelf life ≤ 6 months at import, hexachlorophene, tested on animals after 12 Nov 2014.
- Manufacture: COS-5 (licence) / COS-6 (loan licence) + COS-7 self-declaration → COS-8 / COS-9 within 45 days; inspection within 30 days; perpetual with retention fee; inspection at least once in 3 years.
- Technical staff: D.Pharm / registered pharmacist / Intermediate with chemistry / degree in cosmetic technology, whole-time.
- Records: batch records 3 years after expiry; test records 3 years from manufacture.
- Label: name, manufacturer and address, use before, batch (B.), licence (M.), net contents, ingredients > 1% in descending order, RC number for imports; hair dye caution with patch test; fluoride ≤ 1000 ppm.
- 17C misbranded, 17D spurious, 17E adulterated; section 18 prohibitions; 27A penalties (3 years for spurious/adulterated; 1 year or fine for others).
- Rule 39: IS 4707 Annex A banned; colours from Tenth Schedule (As 2 ppm, Pb 20 ppm, heavy metals 100 ppm); hexachlorophene only in soap ≤ 1%; mercury 70 ppm eye products, 1 ppm unintentional; no animal testing.
