# Unit 2: Biological aspects — skin, hair and oral cavity

Every cosmeceutical is designed backwards from a biological problem: why the skin is dry, why a pore turns into a comedone, why a dark patch forms, why sweat smells, why a tooth decays. This unit gives that biology at the depth needed to choose actives and vehicles in Units 3 and 4. It covers the skin and its common cosmetic problems, the hair and its growth cycle, the oral cavity, and the cleansing and care needs of each body region.

## 2.1 Skin: structure that matters for cosmetics

```text
          Sebum + sweat film ("acid mantle", pH about 4.5–5.5)
 ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
 │ STRATUM CORNEUM  10–20 layers of corneocytes in lipid        │ ◄ barrier, NMF
 │ stratum granulosum  lamellar bodies release lipids           │
 │ stratum spinosum    desmosomes, Langerhans cells             │
 │ stratum basale      keratinocyte stem cells, melanocytes     │ ◄ pigment
 ├─────────────────────── dermo-epidermal junction ─────────────┤
 │ DERMIS  fibroblasts → collagen I/III, elastin, hyaluronan;    │ ◄ wrinkles
 │         vessels, nerves, sebaceous glands, sweat glands,      │
 │         hair follicles                                        │
 ├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
 │ HYPODERMIS  adipocytes                                        │
 └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

**Epidermal turnover.** Basal keratinocytes divide, move upward, fill with keratin and finally lose their nuclei to become flat **corneocytes**, which shed from the surface (desquamation). The journey takes roughly four weeks in young skin and slows with age.

**The stratum corneum barrier ("bricks and mortar").**

- **Bricks** – corneocytes packed with keratin and surrounded by a tough **cornified envelope** (proteins such as loricrin and involucrin, crosslinked by transglutaminase).
- **Mortar** – intercellular lipid lamellae made of **ceramides, cholesterol and free fatty acids** in roughly equimolar amounts. These lipids are secreted from **lamellar bodies** in the granular layer.
- **Natural moisturising factor (NMF)** – water-soluble, hygroscopic molecules inside corneocytes: free amino acids and their derivatives (from breakdown of the protein **filaggrin**), **pyrrolidone carboxylic acid (PCA)**, urocanic acid, lactate, urea and salts. NMF keeps the stratum corneum hydrated and flexible.
- **Desmosomes / corneodesmosomes** hold corneocytes together; proteases break them in a controlled way so cells shed singly and invisibly.

The barrier is measured as **transepidermal water loss (TEWL)**: the higher the TEWL, the weaker the barrier. Healthy stratum corneum holds about 10–20% water; below about 10% it becomes rough and cracks.

**Acid mantle.** The surface pH of about 4.5–5.5 comes from free fatty acids, lactic acid, urocanic acid and the sodium–hydrogen exchanger. An acidic pH keeps barrier enzymes (that make ceramides) active, keeps desquamation enzymes in check, and favours friendly skin bacteria. Alkaline soaps raise surface pH and disturb this balance.

**Skin microbiome.** Staphylococcus epidermidis, Cutibacterium (formerly Propionibacterium), Corynebacterium and Malassezia live on the skin. They occupy space and help defence, but some species cause acne, body odour and dandruff when conditions change.

**Skin types.** Normal, dry, oily, combination and sensitive; Fitzpatrick phototypes I–VI describe how skin burns or tans. Indian skin is mostly types III–V, which tan easily and are prone to pigmentation problems after inflammation.

## 2.2 Skin structure related to common cosmetic problems

### Dry skin (xerosis)

| Cause | Mechanism |
| --- | --- |
| Low humidity, cold, wind | Water evaporates faster than it diffuses up from the dermis |
| Harsh surfactants, hot water, frequent washing | Surfactants dissolve barrier lipids and denature keratin; NMF is washed out; alkaline pH |
| Ageing | Less lipid synthesis, less NMF, slower turnover |
| Genetic (filaggrin defects), atopic tendency | Less NMF, weaker barrier |
| Sun damage, diabetes, hypothyroidism, some drugs | Altered keratinisation |

**What happens:** corneocytes stay stuck together (desquamation enzymes need water), so scales build up; skin feels tight, looks dull and flaky, may crack and itch. The vicious cycle: low water → abnormal shedding → rough surface → more water loss.

### Acne

Acne vulgaris is a disease of the **pilosebaceous unit** (hair follicle with its sebaceous gland), commonest on the face, chest and back during adolescence.

```text
Androgens ↑ ──► sebaceous gland enlarges ──► excess sebum
                                        │
Abnormal keratinisation of the follicle mouth ──► microcomedone
                                        │            │
                                        ▼            ▼
               closed comedone (whitehead)   open comedone (blackhead,
                                             dark due to oxidised lipid
                                             and melanin)
                                        │
Cutibacterium acnes multiplies in sebum ─► lipases → free fatty acids,
                                        │   immune activation
                                        ▼
         Inflammation ──► papules, pustules, nodules ─► scars, post-inflammatory
                                                        hyperpigmentation
```

Four key factors: **(1) increased sebum, (2) follicular hyperkeratinisation, (3) colonisation by C. acnes, (4) inflammation.** Aggravating factors: comedogenic cosmetics (heavy oils and some esters), occlusion, friction, humidity, stress, some foods in susceptible people. Cosmetic products can reduce oil, unblock pores and avoid comedogenicity; moderate to severe acne needs medical treatment.

### Pigmentation

**Melanogenesis.** Melanocytes in the basal layer make melanin inside **melanosomes** and transfer them through dendrites to about 30–40 surrounding keratinocytes (the "epidermal melanin unit").

```text
L-tyrosine ──tyrosinase──► L-DOPA ──tyrosinase──► dopaquinone
                                                     │
                     no cysteine ◄───────────────────┴──────► with cysteine
                         │                                        │
           DHI / DHICA → EUMELANIN                      PHEOMELANIN
           (brown–black)                                (red–yellow)
```

Triggers: **UV light** (DNA damage → α-MSH from keratinocytes → MC1R receptor on melanocytes → more tyrosinase), visible light, inflammation and hormones.

| Disorder | Features |
| --- | --- |
| Melasma | Symmetric brown patches on cheeks, forehead, upper lip; hormones and sun; common in Indian women; relapses easily |
| Post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation | Dark marks after acne, eczema or injury; common in darker skin |
| Solar lentigines | Sun spots on exposed skin in older age |
| Freckles (ephelides) | Small spots that darken in summer |
| Uneven tone, dark circles, tan | Mixed causes |

Cosmeceutical targets: tyrosinase activity, melanosome transfer, turnover of pigmented cells, and sun protection.

### Prickly heat (miliaria)

Miliaria results from **blockage of eccrine sweat ducts** in hot, humid weather, so sweat leaks into the skin.

| Type | Level of blockage | Appearance |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Miliaria crystallina | Within or just under the stratum corneum | Tiny clear blisters, no inflammation |
| Miliaria rubra (prickly heat) | Deeper in the epidermis | Itchy, prickling red papules on trunk, neck, skin folds |
| Miliaria profunda | Dermo-epidermal junction | Flesh-coloured papules, after repeated rubra |

Contributing factors: occlusive clothing, heavy creams, swelling of the stratum corneum from sweat, and bacteria (Staphylococcus) that form slime in ducts. Care: keep skin cool and dry, avoid occlusion, use absorbent and cooling powders.

### Wrinkles and skin ageing

| Intrinsic (chronological) ageing | Extrinsic (photo-)ageing |
| --- | --- |
| Genetic, hormonal (falling oestrogen) | Mainly UV (also pollution, smoking) |
| Fine wrinkles, thin dry skin, loss of fat | Coarse deep wrinkles, leathery texture, spots, broken vessels |
| Less collagen synthesis, slower turnover | UV → reactive oxygen species → activation of **matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs)** that break collagen; reduced new collagen; abnormal elastin (solar elastosis) |
| Gradual loss of hyaluronic acid | **Glycation** (sugar crosslinks) stiffens collagen |

Wrinkles form where the dermis loses collagen and elastin and facial muscles fold the skin repeatedly (expression lines). Cosmeceutical approaches: daily sun protection, retinoids, antioxidants, peptides, AHAs, moisturisers.

### Body odour

| Gland | Location | Secretion | Role in odour |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Eccrine | Whole body, many on palms, soles, forehead | Watery, salty | Mainly wetness; odour on feet when bacteria break down keratin |
| Apocrine | Armpits, groin, areola; active from puberty | Oily, protein- and lipid-rich, odourless when fresh | Bacteria (Corynebacterium, Staphylococcus) convert precursors into volatile fatty acids such as 3-methyl-2-hexenoic acid and sulphur compounds (thioalcohols) and steroid derivatives that smell |

So body odour needs **sweat + bacteria + time**. Control strategies: reduce sweat (antiperspirants), reduce bacteria (antimicrobials, low pH), mask or absorb odour (fragrance, zinc ricinoleate), and good hygiene.

## 2.3 Hair: structure, chemistry and growth cycle

**The follicle.** The hair grows from the **bulb**, where matrix cells divide around the **dermal papilla** (the papilla controls the size and cycle of the hair). Melanocytes in the bulb colour the hair. The sebaceous gland and arrector pili muscle attach to the follicle.

**The shaft.**

| Layer | Structure | Cosmetic importance |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Cuticle | 6–10 layers of flat overlapping scales, tips pointing to the end; outer lipid layer (18-methyleicosanoic acid) makes it water-repellent | Shine, smoothness, combability; damaged by bleaching, alkaline products, heat, friction |
| Cortex | Spindle-shaped cells packed with keratin macrofibrils; holds melanin | Strength and elasticity; site of action of dyes, perms and bleaches |
| Medulla | Loose central core, may be absent | Little cosmetic role |

**Hair chemistry.** Keratin is rich in cystine. Bonds that hold it together:

- **Disulphide bonds** – strong covalent; broken by reducing agents (thioglycolate perms, depilatories) and oxidising bleaches.
- **Hydrogen bonds** – broken by water and reformed on drying (basis of temporary setting).
- **Salt (ionic) bonds** – depend on pH; strongest near the isoelectric point (about pH 3.7).

Hair carries a net **negative charge** at normal pH, more so when damaged, which is why **cationic** conditioners deposit on it.

**Growth cycle.**

| Phase | Events | Approximate duration (scalp) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Anagen | Active growth; about 85–90% of scalp hairs | 2–7 years |
| Catagen | Regression; bulb shrinks | 2–3 weeks |
| Telogen | Rest; club hair held loosely; about 10–15% | About 3 months |
| Exogen | Release of the old hair as the new anagen hair grows | – |

Scalp hair grows about 1 cm a month; losing up to about 100 hairs a day is normal.

**Common hair and scalp problems**

| Problem | Biology |
| --- | --- |
| Androgenetic alopecia | Dihydrotestosterone (made by 5α-reductase) progressively miniaturises follicles and shortens anagen |
| Telogen effluvium | Many follicles enter telogen together after fever, childbirth, crash diet or stress; diffuse shedding 2–3 months later |
| Dandruff / seborrhoeic dermatitis | Malassezia yeasts break sebum triglycerides to irritant free fatty acids (e.g. oleic acid) → inflammation and rapid scaling |
| Greying (canities) | Loss of melanocyte activity in the bulb; oxidative stress |
| Split ends, frizz, breakage | Cuticle loss and weathering |

## 2.4 Oral cavity: structure and common problems

```text
            Enamel (≈96% hydroxyapatite, no living cells)
             │
   ┌─────────▼────────┐
   │      Dentine      │ ◄ tubules filled with fluid, linked to pulp nerves
   │   ┌───────────┐   │
   │   │   Pulp    │   │ ◄ nerves, blood vessels
   └───┴───────────┴───┘
      Gingiva covers bone; cementum covers root
```

**Saliva** buffers acids (bicarbonate), supplies calcium and phosphate for remineralisation, washes away food and carries antibacterial proteins. A thin protein film, the **acquired pellicle**, forms on enamel within minutes of cleaning; bacteria attach to it and grow into **plaque (a biofilm)**.

| Problem | Mechanism |
| --- | --- |
| **Dental caries** | Plaque bacteria (Streptococcus mutans, lactobacilli) ferment sugars to acids; when plaque pH falls below the **critical pH of about 5.5**, enamel hydroxyapatite dissolves (demineralisation). Saliva and fluoride drive remineralisation between meals; frequent sugar intake tips the balance toward cavities |
| **Calculus (tartar)** | Plaque mineralises with calcium phosphate from saliva |
| **Gingivitis (bleeding gums)** | Plaque at the gum line → inflammation; red, swollen gums that bleed on brushing; reversible with good hygiene |
| **Periodontitis** | Inflammation spreads to ligament and bone; pockets, loosening teeth; needs dental care |
| **Halitosis (mouth odour)** | Anaerobic bacteria on the back of the tongue and in gum pockets break down proteins to **volatile sulphur compounds** (hydrogen sulphide, methyl mercaptan) |
| **Dentine hypersensitivity (sensitive teeth)** | Exposed dentine (enamel wear, gum recession, acid erosion) with open tubules; cold, heat, sweet or air moves tubule fluid and stimulates pulp nerves (**hydrodynamic theory**) → short sharp pain |
| **Stains** | Extrinsic (tea, coffee, tobacco, chromogenic bacteria) and intrinsic |
| **Erosion** | Acid from diet or reflux dissolves enamel without bacteria |

## 2.5 Cleansing and care needs of different body regions

| Region | Special biology | Cleansing need | Care need | Typical products |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Face** | Many sebaceous glands (T-zone), thin skin on cheeks, sun-exposed | Remove sebum, sweat, pollution, make-up without stripping lipids; pH-balanced mild surfactants | Moisturise, sun protection, oil control or anti-ageing as needed | Face wash, cleansing milk, micellar water, toner, moisturiser, sunscreen |
| **Eyelids** | Thinnest skin of the body, close to the eye, sensitive | Gentle, non-stinging; remove waterproof make-up with oils or biphasic removers | Light non-irritant creams; ophthalmologist-tested | Eye make-up remover, eye cream/gel |
| **Lips** | No sebaceous glands, very thin stratum corneum, no melanin protection to speak of | Water is enough | Occlusive balms, UV protection | Lip balm, lipstick with emollients |
| **Hands** | Frequent washing and detergents, exposed to sun | Mild hand washes | Barrier creams, hand creams with humectants and occlusives | Hand wash, hand cream |
| **Feet** | Thick stratum corneum on soles, many eccrine glands, enclosed in shoes | Wash and dry between toes | Keratolytic softening of heels (urea, salicylic acid), antifungal and deodorant powders | Foot cream, foot powder |
| **Nails** | Hard keratin plate; brittle with detergents and solvents | Gentle cleaning; avoid harsh removers | Moisturise cuticles; nail hardeners | Nail polish, remover, cuticle cream |
| **Scalp** | Dense follicles, high sebum, Malassezia | Shampoo to remove sebum, scales and styling residue | Conditioning, anti-dandruff, scalp tonics | Shampoo, conditioner, hair oil |
| **Neck** | Thin skin, sun-exposed, shows ageing | Like face | Moisturiser, sunscreen | Same as face products |
| **Body** | Fewer sebaceous glands on limbs; legs prone to dryness | Mild bath products, syndet bars | Body lotion, especially after bath | Soap/syndet, body wash, lotion |
| **Under-arm** | Apocrine glands, occlusion, hair, friction | Wash with mild cleanser | Control sweat and odour without irritation | Deodorant, antiperspirant |

## Remember

- Stratum corneum = bricks (corneocytes) and mortar (ceramides, cholesterol, free fatty acids); NMF from filaggrin keeps it hydrated; TEWL measures barrier.
- Acid mantle pH about 4.5–5.5 supports barrier enzymes and friendly microbes.
- Dry skin: lipid and NMF loss → abnormal desquamation → scaling.
- Acne: sebum ↑, follicular hyperkeratinisation, C. acnes, inflammation.
- Melanin: tyrosine → DOPA → dopaquinone (tyrosinase) → eumelanin or pheomelanin; UV → α-MSH → MC1R.
- Miliaria = blocked eccrine ducts: crystallina, rubra (prickly heat), profunda.
- Photoageing: UV → ROS → MMPs → collagen breakdown; glycation stiffens collagen.
- Body odour: apocrine secretion + skin bacteria → volatile fatty acids and thioalcohols.
- Hair: cuticle, cortex, medulla; disulphide, hydrogen and salt bonds; negative charge; anagen 2–7 years, catagen 2–3 weeks, telogen about 3 months.
- Dandruff = Malassezia + sebum; androgenetic alopecia = DHT miniaturisation.
- Caries below critical pH about 5.5; gingivitis from plaque; halitosis from volatile sulphur compounds; sensitivity by the hydrodynamic theory.

# Unit 3: Formulation building blocks, perfumes and controversial ingredients

Most cosmetics are built from a small set of ingredient families combined in different proportions. A cold cream and a vanishing cream use similar oils and waxes; a shampoo and a face wash share surfactants; almost every water-containing product needs the same preservative thinking. This unit treats those families as **building blocks**: what each one does, how it is classified, and how the blocks are assembled into classic products. It ends with perfumes, the fragrance allergens named in EU law, and three ingredient groups that attract public controversy.

## 3.1 The building-block approach

```text
                      FINISHED COSMETIC
   ┌──────────────┬───────────────┬───────────────┬───────────────┐
   │ Vehicle /    │ Functional    │ Actives       │ Stabilising & │
   │ base         │ excipients    │ (claims)      │ sensory       │
   ├──────────────┼───────────────┼───────────────┼───────────────┤
   │ water, oils, │ surfactants,  │ moisturisers, │ preservatives,│
   │ alcohols,    │ emulsifiers,  │ UV filters,   │ antioxidants, │
   │ powders      │ thickeners    │ fluoride,     │ chelators, pH │
   │              │               │ anti-dandruff │ adjusters,    │
   │              │               │ agents …      │ colour, scent │
   └──────────────┴───────────────┴───────────────┴───────────────┘
```

Choosing blocks starts from the **target product profile**: skin/hair type, the claim, sensory feel (light, rich, non-greasy), format (cream, gel, stick, bar), pack (jar, tube, pump, aerosol), cost, regulatory lists (BIS IS 4707, permitted colours) and stability (shelf life usually 24–36 months).

## 3.2 Surfactants: classification and application

A surfactant has a **hydrophilic head** and a **lipophilic tail**. Above the **critical micelle concentration (CMC)** molecules associate into micelles that hold oil and dirt. Useful concepts:

| Concept | Meaning | Formulation use |
| --- | --- | --- |
| CMC | Concentration at which micelles form; above it surface tension stops falling | Lower CMC = efficient, often milder (fewer free monomers) |
| Krafft point | Temperature below which an ionic surfactant is too insoluble to form micelles | Soaps of long saturated acids need warm water; important for clear liquids |
| HLB (Griffin) | Hydrophilic–lipophilic balance on a 0–20 scale; for polyoxyethylene esters HLB = E/5 (E = % ethylene oxide by weight); for fatty acid esters HLB = 20(1 − S/A) | 3–6 w/o emulsifiers; 7–9 wetting agents; 8–18 o/w emulsifiers; 13–15 detergents; 15–18 solubilisers |
| Required HLB | The HLB an oil phase needs for a stable emulsion | Blend emulsifiers: HLB(mix) = f·HLB(A) + (1 − f)·HLB(B) |
| Critical packing parameter | P = v/(a0·lc): < 1/3 spherical micelles, 1/3–1/2 rods, 1/2–1 bilayers, > 1 reverse micelles | Explains why some surfactants thicken (rod micelles) or form liposome-like structures |

**Classification by charge of the head group**

| Class | Examples | Properties | Applications |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Anionic** | Soaps (sodium/potassium salts of fatty acids), sodium lauryl sulphate (SLS), sodium laureth sulphate (SLES), ammonium lauryl sulphate, alpha-olefin sulphonate, sodium cocoyl isethionate (SCI), sodium lauroyl sarcosinate, sodium cocoyl glutamate, sulphosuccinates | Strong cleansing and foaming; may irritate (SLS > SLES > acyl amino acids); sensitive to hard water (soaps) | Shampoos, body and face washes, toothpaste (SLS as foaming agent), syndet bars |
| **Cationic** | Quaternary ammonium compounds: cetrimonium chloride, behentrimonium chloride/methosulphate, distearyldimonium chloride; esterquats; benzalkonium chloride, cetylpyridinium chloride | Adsorb on negatively charged hair and skin; conditioning, anti-static; antimicrobial; little foam; can irritate eyes | Hair conditioners, antimicrobial mouthwash (CPC), preservative (benzalkonium) |
| **Amphoteric (zwitterionic)** | Cocamidopropyl betaine, coco betaine, sodium lauroamphoacetate, hydroxysultaines | Charge depends on pH; mild; boost foam and viscosity; reduce irritation of anionics | Baby shampoos, mild washes, secondary surfactant |
| **Non-ionic** | Fatty alcohol ethoxylates (ceteareth-20, laureth-4), polysorbates, sorbitan esters, glyceryl stearate, PEG esters, alkyl polyglucosides (decyl/coco glucoside), fatty acid alkanolamides (cocamide MEA), sucrose esters, poloxamers | Not affected by hard water or charge; good emulsifiers and solubilisers; usually mild; may inactivate some preservatives | Creams and lotions (emulsifiers), perfume solubilisers in toners, mild cleansers, foam stabilisers |

**Applications by function**

| Function | Typical surfactants |
| --- | --- |
| Primary cleanser / foamer | SLES, SLS, SCI, alpha-olefin sulphonate |
| Secondary (mildness, foam, viscosity) | Cocamidopropyl betaine, alkyl polyglucosides, cocamide MEA |
| O/W emulsifier | Ceteareth-20, polysorbate 60, glyceryl stearate + PEG-100 stearate, cetearyl glucoside |
| W/O emulsifier | Sorbitan oleate, polyglyceryl-3 diisostearate, PEG-30 dipolyhydroxystearate, beeswax–borax (in situ soap) |
| Solubiliser | Polysorbate 20, PEG-40 hydrogenated castor oil |
| Conditioner | Behentrimonium chloride, polyquaternium-10 (cationic polymer) |
| Wetting agent / dispersant | Low-HLB to mid-HLB non-ionics, sarcosinates |

**Mildness** is assessed by protein denaturation (the **zein test** measures dissolved corn protein), irritation tests on reconstructed epidermis, and TEWL after repeated washing. Mixed micelles (anionic + amphoteric or non-ionic) lower the free-monomer concentration and so reduce irritation.

## 3.3 Emollients: classification and application

Emollients are oily or waxy materials that make the skin soft and smooth by filling spaces between desquamating corneocytes; many also reduce water loss (**occlusives**). Moisturisers combine **emollients, occlusives and humectants**.

**Classification by chemistry**

| Group | Examples | Feel and use |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Hydrocarbons | Mineral oil, petrolatum, microcrystalline wax, squalane, hydrogenated polyisobutene | Petrolatum is the most occlusive (reduces TEWL by about 98%); heavy feel; inexpensive |
| Triglycerides (vegetable oils and butters) | Almond, olive, sunflower, coconut, jojoba (actually a wax ester), shea butter, cocoa butter, caprylic/capric triglyceride | Nourishing, may oxidise (need antioxidants); rich feel |
| Esters (synthetic) | Isopropyl myristate, isopropyl palmitate, C12–15 alkyl benzoate, cetearyl ethylhexanoate, ethylhexyl palmitate | Light, fast spreading; some (isopropyl myristate) can be comedogenic; good solvents for UV filters |
| Fatty alcohols | Cetyl, stearyl, cetostearyl, behenyl alcohol | Body, stability and "soaping" feel in creams; co-emulsifiers |
| Fatty acids | Stearic, palmitic, myristic | Vanishing creams, soaps, cleansing creams |
| Silicones | Dimethicone, cyclopentasiloxane (volatile; its use is being restricted in the EU for environmental reasons), amodimethicone | Silky, non-greasy, breathable film; hair shine and conditioning |
| Lanolin and derivatives | Lanolin, lanolin alcohols, acetylated lanolin | Excellent emollient; possible allergy in some users |
| Waxes | Beeswax, carnauba, candelilla, ceresin | Structure for sticks and balms |
| Skin-identical lipids | Ceramides, cholesterol, free fatty acids, phytosphingosine | Barrier repair in dry or atopic skin |

**Classification by spreading and feel:** fast-spreading (volatile silicones, light esters) → medium (isopropyl myristate, triglycerides) → slow-spreading, rich (petrolatum, butters, lanolin). Formulators often use an **emollient cascade** – a blend of fast, medium and slow emollients – to give a pleasant feel that changes during rub-in.

**Selection criteria:** polarity (affects emulsion stability and solubility of actives), spreading value, occlusivity, comedogenicity, oxidative stability, odour and colour, compatibility with UV filters, regulatory and natural-certification status, cost.

## 3.4 Rheological additives: classification and application

**Why rheology matters:** viscosity gives the product body; **shear-thinning** (pseudoplastic) flow lets a lotion pour or a cream spread easily while it stays thick at rest; a **yield value** keeps particles and droplets suspended; **thixotropy** lets a gel recover after shaking.

| Class | Examples | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Natural gums and polysaccharides | Xanthan gum, guar gum, carrageenan, gum acacia, gellan, sclerotium gum, alginates, starches | Tolerate salts; xanthan has a high yield value; may feel slightly sticky |
| Semi-synthetic (cellulose derivatives) | Sodium carboxymethylcellulose, hydroxyethylcellulose, hydroxypropylmethylcellulose, methylcellulose | Clear gels; CMC is the classic toothpaste binder |
| Synthetic polymers | Carbomers (crosslinked polyacrylic acid), acrylates/C10–30 alkyl acrylate crosspolymer, sodium polyacrylate, polyacrylamide-type thickeners | Need neutralisation (carbomers) to swell; crystal-clear gels; sensitive to electrolytes |
| Associative thickeners | Hydrophobically modified polymers (HASE types, PEG-150 distearate) | Thicken surfactant systems by linking micelles |
| Electrolytes | Sodium chloride, ammonium chloride | Thicken SLES/betaine shampoos by growing rod micelles; viscosity rises then falls past a "salt curve" maximum |
| Inorganic clays and silicas | Bentonite, magnesium aluminium silicate, hectorite, fumed silica, hydrated silica | Gel structure, suspension, mattifying; silica thickens toothpaste |
| Lipid thickeners | Fatty alcohols, waxes, hydrogenated castor oil, stearic acid | Structure creams (liquid-crystal gel networks) and anhydrous sticks |

**Application examples:** carbomer for clear facial gels; xanthan + fatty alcohol for creams; salt for shampoos; CMC or xanthan + silica for toothpaste; clays for face packs and suspensions of zinc oxide.

## 3.5 Antimicrobials used as preservatives

Water, nutrients (proteins, sugars, plant extracts) and repeated opening make cosmetics ideal for microbes. Contamination can spoil the product (odour, colour change, emulsion breaking) and harm users, especially near the eyes. Preservatives protect against contamination **during use**; they do not replace GMP.

**Ideal preservative:** broad spectrum (Gram-positive and Gram-negative bacteria, yeasts, moulds); effective at low concentration across the product's pH; partitions into the water phase; stable to heat and storage; compatible with ingredients and packaging; non-toxic, non-irritant, non-sensitising; colourless and odourless; permitted by regulation; affordable.

| Preservative | Merits | Demerits |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Parabens (methyl, ethyl, propyl, butyl esters of p-hydroxybenzoic acid) | Broad spectrum (esp. fungi), effective from pH about 3–8, long safety record, cheap | Lower activity with increasing chain length in water; bound by non-ionics; public concern over endocrine effects (see 3.10); some long-chain esters banned in EU |
| Phenoxyethanol | Broad, stable, compatible | Weak against some moulds and Pseudomonas alone; used with boosters (ethylhexylglycerin) |
| Organic acids: benzoic acid/sodium benzoate, sorbic acid/potassium sorbate, dehydroacetic acid | Mild, accepted in natural products | Work only in **undissociated form** at low pH (about ≤ 5.5); weak against bacteria |
| Benzyl alcohol | Mild, accepted in natural products | Weak; odour; listed fragrance allergen |
| Formaldehyde releasers (DMDM hydantoin, imidazolidinyl urea, diazolidinyl urea, quaternium-15, bronopol) | Very effective against bacteria, cheap | Sensitisation; formaldehyde concerns (see 3.10) |
| Isothiazolinones (methylchloroisothiazolinone/methylisothiazolinone) | Very active at ppm levels, broad | High rates of contact allergy; restricted to rinse-off products in the EU |
| Quaternary ammonium compounds (benzalkonium chloride) | Active against bacteria | Inactivated by anionics; eye irritation |
| Chlorphenesin, o-cymen-5-ol, piroctone olamine | Useful partners | Limited spectrum alone |
| Multifunctional "preservative-free" boosters (caprylyl glycol, glyceryl caprylate, ethylhexylglycerin, 1,2-hexanediol) | Support preservation, not listed as preservatives in some markets | Need higher levels; may affect feel |

Preservatives are usually combined to widen the spectrum and allow lower levels of each.

## 3.6 Factors affecting preservative efficacy

1. **pH and pKa.** Weak-acid preservatives act in the undissociated form; efficacy falls sharply when pH exceeds pKa (benzoic acid pKa about 4.2, sorbic acid about 4.8).
2. **Oil–water partition.** Microbes grow in the water phase; a lipophilic preservative (long-chain paraben) migrates into oil and leaves too little in water. Effective concentration in water depends on the oil:water ratio and the partition coefficient.
3. **Binding to surfactants (micellar solubilisation).** Non-ionic surfactants such as polysorbates bind parabens and phenols in micelles, so the free (active) fraction drops; a higher total level is then needed.
4. **Interaction with other ingredients.** Cationic preservatives are inactivated by anionic surfactants; proteins, cellulose derivatives, powders (talc, kaolin, titanium dioxide) and plant extracts can adsorb or inactivate preservatives.
5. **Packaging.** Preservatives can sorb into or permeate plastics and rubber; open jars expose product to fingers and air, whereas airless pumps and tubes reduce contamination.
6. **Water activity (aw).** Microbes need free water; high glycerin, sugar or salt content and anhydrous products lower aw (most bacteria need aw above about 0.9).
7. **Temperature and storage time.** Preservatives may degrade or evaporate; heat during manufacture can hydrolyse esters.
8. **Initial microbial load.** Contaminated water, raw materials (especially natural ones) or poor hygiene can overwhelm any preservative – GMP comes first.
9. **Product structure.** Multiple emulsions, high-viscosity regions and solid particles can create pockets where preservative is low.
10. **Synergy and boosters.** Chelating agents (disodium EDTA) weaken Gram-negative cell walls; glycols and alcohol contribute activity; combinations allow a "hurdle" approach (low pH + low aw + preservative + good packaging).

**Preservative efficacy (challenge) test.** The product is inoculated separately with standard organisms – *Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Staphylococcus aureus, Escherichia coli, Candida albicans* and *Aspergillus brasiliensis* – and the count is followed over 28 days (for example at 7, 14 and 28 days). The internationally used cosmetic method is **ISO 11930**, which sets criteria for log reduction of bacteria and fungi. A product that fails is reformulated or packed in protective packaging.

## 3.7 Building blocks of classic products

The formulas below show the **type and typical range** of each block, not a licensed recipe.

### Moisturising cream (o/w)

| Block | Examples | Typical % |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Water phase | Purified water | to 100 |
| Humectants | Glycerin, propylene glycol, sorbitol, sodium PCA, urea | 3–10 |
| Emollients / occlusives | Light liquid paraffin, caprylic/capric triglyceride, isopropyl myristate, dimethicone, shea butter | 10–25 |
| Consistency factors | Cetostearyl alcohol, stearic acid, glyceryl stearate | 2–6 |
| Emulsifiers | Ceteareth-20, glyceryl stearate SE, cetearyl glucoside | 2–5 |
| Thickener | Xanthan gum or carbomer (neutralised) | 0.2–0.5 |
| Barrier actives | Ceramides, niacinamide, panthenol, allantoin | 0.1–5 |
| Preservative, chelator, antioxidant | Phenoxyethanol, disodium EDTA, tocopherol | as permitted |
| Perfume, pH adjuster | – | small |

Method: heat oil phase and water phase separately to about 70–75 °C, add the oil to water (or water to oil) with homogenisation, cool with stirring, add heat-sensitive actives, perfume and preservative below about 40 °C, adjust pH (about 5–6).

### Vanishing cream (o/w, stearate type)

A cream that "vanishes" on rubbing, leaving a dry, matt, non-greasy film – because its oil phase is mainly **stearic acid**, part of which is neutralised to a soap that acts as the emulsifier.

| Block | Examples | Typical % |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Fatty acid | Stearic acid (triple-pressed) | 15–25 |
| Alkali (forms soap in situ) | Potassium hydroxide, sodium hydroxide or triethanolamine (neutralising about 15–25% of the stearic acid) | about 0.5–1 |
| Humectant | Glycerin, sorbitol | 5–10 |
| Others | Cetyl alcohol (body), preservative, perfume | small |
| Water | Purified water | to 100 |

The unneutralised stearic acid crystallises into fine plates that give a **pearly lustre** after ageing. Used as a day cream and make-up base.

### Cold cream (w/o, beeswax–borax type)

A cream that gives a **cooling** sensation as its water evaporates, used for cleansing and as a night/massage cream.

| Block | Examples | Typical % |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Wax | White beeswax | 10–20 |
| Oil | Liquid paraffin, almond oil | 40–55 |
| Emulsifier formed in situ | Borax reacts with free cerotic acid of beeswax to form sodium cerotate | 0.5–1 |
| Water | Purified water, rose water | 20–35 |
| Preservative, antioxidant, perfume | – | small |

Beeswax–borax creams are usually w/o; with a high water content and the right borax ratio they can invert to o/w. Modern cold creams also use w/o emulsifiers such as polyglyceryl esters.

### Shampoo

| Block | Examples | Typical % |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Primary surfactant | SLES, ammonium lauryl sulphate, alpha-olefin sulphonate, SCI (sulphate-free) | 8–15 (active) |
| Secondary surfactant / foam booster | Cocamidopropyl betaine, cocamide MEA, coco glucoside | 2–5 |
| Conditioning agents | Polyquaternium-10, guar hydroxypropyltrimonium chloride, dimethicone, panthenol | 0.1–2 |
| Thickener | Sodium chloride, PEG-150 distearate, acrylates copolymer | 0.5–3 |
| Pearlising / opacifier | Glycol distearate | 0.5–2 |
| Actives | Zinc pyrithione, piroctone olamine, climbazole (anti-dandruff); suspended with acrylate polymers | as permitted |
| pH adjuster | Citric acid (pH about 5–6.5) | q.s. |
| Preservative, chelator, perfume, colour | – | small |
| Water | – | to 100 |

"Two-in-one" (conditioning) shampoos rely on **coacervate deposition**: cationic polymer and anionic surfactant form a complex that separates on dilution during rinsing and deposits silicone onto hair.

### Toothpaste

| Block | Examples | Typical % |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Abrasive (cleaning, stain removal) | Calcium carbonate, dicalcium phosphate dihydrate, hydrated silica, alumina | 20–50 |
| Humectant (stops drying in the tube) | Sorbitol, glycerin, PEG | 20–40 |
| Binder / thickener | Sodium CMC, xanthan, carrageenan, thickening silica | 0.5–2 |
| Foaming agent | Sodium lauryl sulphate, cocamidopropyl betaine | 1–2 |
| Active | Sodium fluoride or sodium monofluorophosphate (fluoride ≤ 1000 ppm in India), potassium nitrate (sensitivity), zinc citrate (tartar, gums) | as permitted |
| Sweetener, flavour | Sodium saccharin; peppermint, spearmint, menthol | small |
| Preservative, colour, water | Sodium benzoate or parabens | small, to 100 |

Abrasivity is controlled (relative dentine abrasivity) so the paste cleans without wearing dentine. Fluoride must stay **available**: calcium carbonate abrasives bind free sodium fluoride, so they are paired with monofluorophosphate; silica is compatible with sodium fluoride.

## 3.8 Soaps and syndet bars

**Soap** = alkali-metal salt of long-chain fatty acids, made by **saponification**:

```text
Triglyceride + 3 NaOH  ──►  Glycerol + 3 RCOONa (soap)
(fat / oil)                            (hard bar with Na; soft/liquid with K)
```

| Raw material | Contribution |
| --- | --- |
| Tallow or palm oil (C16–C18) | Hardness, long-lasting creamy lather, mild |
| Coconut or palm kernel oil (C12–C14) | Quick, abundant lather, more soluble; more drying |
| Typical blend | About 80:20 tallow/palm : coconut |

Processes: full boiling (kettle), cold process, semi-boiled, and continuous saponification or neutralisation of fatty acids. Toilet soaps are milled, plodded and stamped; additives include glycerin, perfume, colour, antioxidant (to prevent rancidity) and chelator. BIS grades toilet soaps by **total fatty matter (TFM)**: Grade 1 at least 76%, Grade 2 at least 70%, Grade 3 at least 60%.

Drawbacks of soap: **alkaline pH (about 9–10)**, forms insoluble calcium and magnesium soaps (scum) in hard water, removes barrier lipids and swells the stratum corneum, which can dry and irritate the skin.

**Syndet bars** (synthetic detergent bars) are based mainly on mild synthetic surfactants, chiefly **sodium cocoyl isethionate**, plus stearic acid, paraffin or fatty alcohols as plasticisers and binders, with fillers (starch, dextrin) and emollients. **Combars** combine soap and syndet.

| Property | Soap | Syndet bar |
| --- | --- | --- |
| pH of solution | About 9–10 | About 5.5–7 |
| Hard water | Scum | No scum |
| Effect on barrier | More lipid and protein damage | Milder; less TEWL rise |
| Lather | Good | Creamy, slightly less |
| Wear and mush | Usually lower mush | Needs careful formulation |
| Cost | Low | Higher |
| Best for | Normal skin | Dry, sensitive, acne-prone, atopic skin, babies |

## 3.9 Perfumes

**Classification by origin**

| Source | Examples |
| --- | --- |
| Natural plant materials (essential oils, absolutes, resinoids) | Rose, jasmine, sandalwood, vetiver, lavender, citrus oils, patchouli |
| Animal (now replaced by synthetics) | Musk, civet, ambergris, castoreum |
| Synthetic and nature-identical aroma chemicals | Linalool, citronellol, geraniol, hexyl cinnamal, coumarin, vanillin, Iso E Super-type woody materials, macrocyclic and polycyclic musks |

**Classification by olfactory family** (fragrance wheel): **floral** (single flower, floral bouquet), **fresh** (citrus, green, aquatic, aromatic), **oriental/amber** (vanilla, resins, spices), **woody** (sandalwood, cedar, vetiver), **chypre** (citrus top on oakmoss–patchouli base), **fougère** (lavender, coumarin, oakmoss – typical of men's fragrances), and gourmand.

**Classification by concentration of perfume oil** (typical ranges, not legal limits)

| Type | Perfume concentrate |
| --- | --- |
| Parfum / extrait | About 20–30% |
| Eau de parfum | About 15–20% |
| Eau de toilette | About 5–15% |
| Eau de cologne | About 2–5% |
| Body mist / splash | About 1–3% |

**Structure of a perfume (notes)**

```text
 TOP notes     │ smelled first, evaporate in minutes  │ citrus, light herbs, aldehydes
 MIDDLE (heart)│ the character, last hours             │ floral, spices
 BASE notes    │ fixatives, last longest               │ woods, musks, vanilla, resins
```

**Perfuming cosmetics:** the fragrance must suit the base (alkaline soaps destroy some esters), not discolour (vanillin and indole darken in some bases), be solubilised in clear products, and stay within allergen and safety limits. The International Fragrance Association (IFRA) issues industry standards that restrict or ban certain fragrance materials by product category.

### Perfume ingredients listed as allergens in EU regulation

Under Regulation (EC) No 1223/2009, Annex III lists fragrance substances that are known contact allergens. They must be **named in the ingredient list** when present above **0.001% in leave-on** or **0.01% in rinse-off** products. The original list has **26 substances**:

| Type | Substances |
| --- | --- |
| Aroma chemicals (24) | Amyl cinnamal, amylcinnamyl alcohol, anise alcohol, benzyl alcohol, benzyl benzoate, benzyl cinnamate, benzyl salicylate, cinnamal, cinnamyl alcohol, citral, citronellol, coumarin, eugenol, farnesol, geraniol, hexyl cinnamal, hydroxycitronellal, hydroxyisohexyl 3-cyclohexene carboxaldehyde (HICC), isoeugenol, limonene, linalool, methyl 2-octynoate, alpha-isomethyl ionone, butylphenyl methylpropional (lilial) |
| Natural extracts (2) | Oakmoss extract (Evernia prunastri), treemoss extract (Evernia furfuracea) |

Later changes students should know:

- **HICC** and the oakmoss/treemoss sensitisers **atranol and chloroatranol** have been **banned** in the EU because of their high allergy rates.
- **Butylphenyl methylpropional (lilial)** was banned in 2022 after classification as toxic to reproduction.
- **Regulation (EU) 2023/1545** expanded the list of fragrance allergens requiring labelling to about 80 substances (adding many essential-oil allergens and further aroma chemicals), with transition periods; new products had to comply from 31 July 2026.

Formulators in India follow these lists voluntarily or when exporting; they are also a good guide to safer fragrance design for sensitive-skin products.

## 3.10 Controversial ingredients

### Parabens

**Concern:** weak oestrogen-like activity in laboratory tests (much weaker than oestradiol; increases with chain length) and a much-publicised 2004 study that detected parabens in breast tumour tissue (it did not show that parabens caused cancer).

**Scientific and regulatory position (EU):**

| Paraben | Status |
| --- | --- |
| Methylparaben, ethylparaben | Permitted up to 0.4% (as acid) for a single ester and 0.8% for mixtures of esters |
| Propylparaben, butylparaben | Permitted, total not more than 0.14% (as acid); not allowed in leave-on products for the nappy area of children under 3 years |
| Isopropyl-, isobutyl-, phenyl-, benzyl- and pentylparaben | Banned (insufficient safety data) |

**Formulator's view:** short-chain parabens remain among the best-studied, least sensitising preservatives. "Paraben-free" products often swap them for alternatives (isothiazolinones, formaldehyde releasers) that have **higher** allergy rates – a point examiners like to see.

### Formaldehyde and formaldehyde liberators

Formaldehyde is a known sensitiser and is classified as carcinogenic (category 1B) in the EU. Direct use as a preservative has been withdrawn in the EU; it may still be present as a **released** substance. **Formaldehyde liberators** (DMDM hydantoin, imidazolidinyl urea, diazolidinyl urea, quaternium-15, sodium hydroxymethylglycinate, bronopol) slowly release formaldehyde in water-based products.

| Issue | Detail |
| --- | --- |
| Allergy | Common cause of contact dermatitis in sensitised users |
| Labelling (EU) | Regulation (EU) 2022/1181 requires the warning **"releases formaldehyde"** when total formaldehyde released by all releasers exceeds **0.001% (10 ppm)** (earlier threshold 0.05%); applied to new products from 31 July 2024 and to all products from 31 July 2026 |
| Hair-smoothing ("keratin") treatments | Some release formaldehyde gas on heating with irons – an inhalation and eye hazard for salon workers |
| Bronopol | Can form nitrosamines with amines in the formula |

### 1,4-Dioxane

1,4-Dioxane is **not added deliberately**; it is a **by-product of ethoxylation** (made from ethylene oxide) and appears as a trace impurity in ethoxylated ingredients such as SLES, PEGs, polysorbates and ceteths. It is classified as a possible human carcinogen.

Control measures:

1. **Vacuum stripping** of ethoxylated raw materials by the supplier.
2. Specifying low dioxane limits in raw-material specifications and testing (headspace GC–MS).
3. Using non-ethoxylated alternatives (sulphates without ether, acyl isethionates, alkyl polyglucosides, amino-acid surfactants).

In the EU 1,4-dioxane is a prohibited substance; only technically unavoidable traces from raw materials are tolerated if the product is safe. Some regulators outside Europe (for example, New York State in the USA) have set numerical limits on dioxane in personal care products.

**Teaching point:** "controversial" ingredients are judged by **hazard, exposure and risk**. An ingredient may be hazardous yet safe at the low levels used; the formulator's job is to document the margin of safety (Unit 4) and to avoid replacing a well-understood ingredient with a poorly studied one.

## Remember

- Building blocks: vehicle + functional excipients + actives + stabilisers/sensory; start from the target product profile.
- Surfactants: anionic (cleanse, foam), cationic (condition, antimicrobial), amphoteric (mild, booster), non-ionic (emulsify, solubilise). HLB 3–6 w/o, 8–18 o/w, 15–18 solubilisers; packing parameter predicts micelle shape.
- Emollients: hydrocarbons, triglycerides, esters, fatty alcohols/acids, silicones, lanolin, waxes, skin-identical lipids; petrolatum most occlusive.
- Rheology: gums, cellulose derivatives, carbomers (neutralise), associative polymers, salt (shampoos), clays/silica, fatty alcohols; shear-thinning with yield value is ideal.
- Preservative efficacy depends on pH (undissociated acid), oil–water partition, micellar binding by non-ionics, interactions, packaging, aw, load, structure; test by challenge test (ISO 11930), 28 days, five organisms.
- Vanishing cream = stearic acid partly neutralised (o/w, pearly); cold cream = beeswax–borax (w/o, cooling).
- Toothpaste: abrasive + humectant + binder + SLS + fluoride (≤ 1000 ppm India) + flavour; CaCO3 pairs with MFP.
- Soap pH 9–10, TFM grades 76/70/60%; syndet (SCI) pH 5.5–7, milder.
- Perfume: by origin, family, concentration (parfum 20–30% … cologne 2–5%), notes top/heart/base.
- EU allergens: 26 listed, label above 0.001% leave-on / 0.01% rinse-off; expanded to about 80 by Regulation 2023/1545; HICC, atranol, chloroatranol, lilial banned.
- Parabens: methyl/ethyl 0.4%/0.8%; propyl + butyl ≤ 0.14% total; five long/branched parabens banned (EU).
- Formaldehyde releasers: "releases formaldehyde" above 0.001% (Reg. 2022/1181). 1,4-dioxane: ethoxylation by-product, removed by vacuum stripping.

# Unit 4: Design of cosmeceutical products, with safety and efficacy evaluation

A cosmeceutical is designed in three steps: **understand the biology of the problem** (Unit 2), **choose actives that act on that biology at permitted cosmetic levels**, and **build a vehicle that delivers them, keeps them stable and feels pleasant** (Unit 3). This unit applies that method to sun protection and to the problems named in the syllabus – dry skin, acne, pigmentation, prickly heat, wrinkles, body odour, dandruff, dental cavities, bleeding gums, mouth odour and sensitive teeth – and ends with how such products are tested for safety and efficacy.

> Regulatory reminder: in India a product claiming to **treat** acne, melasma, dandruff disease, gum disease or alopecia is a **drug**. Cosmeceutical claims are worded as care and appearance claims (for example "helps reduce the look of blemishes", "helps reduce plaque"). Actives such as hydroquinone, tretinoin, benzoyl peroxide, ketoconazole, minoxidil and clindamycin are regulated as drugs.

## 4.1 General design principles

| Step | Questions to answer |
| --- | --- |
| Target and claim | Which problem, which skin/hair type, which wording is permitted? |
| Active selection | Mechanism, effective and permitted concentration, pH of stability and activity, solubility, penetration needed (surface, stratum corneum, epidermis, follicle) |
| Vehicle | Emulsion, gel, serum, foam, stick; occlusion level; non-comedogenic for oily skin |
| Delivery | Penetration enhancers (glycols), encapsulation (liposomes, niosomes, nanostructured lipid carriers, microsponges, cyclodextrins) to improve stability, targeting or tolerance |
| Stability | Oxidation (vitamin C, retinol), light (avobenzone), hydrolysis; antioxidants, chelators, airless/opaque packs |
| Safety | Irritation (acids, retinoids), sensitisation, phototoxicity; margin of safety |
| Proof | Instrumental and clinical claim substantiation (section 4.9) |

## 4.2 Sun protection and sunscreens

### UV radiation and its effects

| Band | Wavelength | Effects |
| --- | --- | --- |
| UVC | 100–280 nm | Absorbed by ozone; does not reach the ground |
| UVB | 280 (290)–320 nm | Sunburn (erythema), DNA damage (thymine dimers), skin cancer, delayed tanning, vitamin D synthesis |
| UVA2 | 320–340 nm | Tanning, photoageing |
| UVA1 | 340–400 nm | Penetrates to the dermis; ROS, MMP activation, photoageing, pigmentation, photosensitivity reactions; passes through glass |
| Visible (especially blue light) and infrared | 400–700 nm and above | Visible light worsens pigmentation (melasma) in darker skin; infrared adds heat and ROS |

### Classification of sunscreens

**1. By mechanism**

| Type | How it works | Examples | Points |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Organic (chemical, "UV absorbers") | Conjugated molecules absorb UV and release the energy as heat | See table below | Transparent, elegant; some photounstable or sensitising |
| Inorganic (physical, mineral) | Particles absorb and scatter UV (and some visible light) | Zinc oxide (UVB + UVA1), titanium dioxide (UVB + UVA2) | Photostable, low allergy; whitening unless micronised/nano; coated to prevent photocatalysis |
| Systemic/oral photoprotectives | Antioxidants taken by mouth | Polypodium leucotomos extract, carotenoids | Only supplementary |

**2. By chemical class (organic filters)**

| Class | Examples | Range |
| --- | --- | --- |
| p-Aminobenzoates | PABA, padimate O | UVB (PABA now little used: allergy, staining) |
| Cinnamates | Octinoxate (ethylhexyl methoxycinnamate), cinoxate | UVB |
| Salicylates | Octisalate (ethylhexyl salicylate), homosalate | UVB (weak; also solvents) |
| Others | Octocrylene, ensulizole (phenylbenzimidazole sulphonic acid, water-soluble) | UVB |
| Benzophenones | Oxybenzone (benzophenone-3), sulisobenzone | UVB + UVA2 |
| Dibenzoylmethanes | Avobenzone (butyl methoxydibenzoylmethane) | UVA1 – photounstable; stabilised with octocrylene or bemotrizinol |
| Anthranilates | Meradimate | UVA2 |
| Newer broad-spectrum (largely EU/Asia) | Bemotrizinol (bis-ethylhexyloxyphenol methoxyphenyl triazine), bisoctrizole (methylene bis-benzotriazolyl tetramethylbutylphenol), ecamsule (terephthalylidene dicamphor sulphonic acid), drometrizole trisiloxane, diethylamino hydroxybenzoyl hexyl benzoate | UVB + UVA |

**3. By protection claim:** UVB only (sunburn), broad spectrum (UVB + UVA), water-resistant, products with added visible-light protection (tinted with iron oxides).

### Rating sun protection

- **SPF** = MED (minimal erythema dose) of protected skin ÷ MED of unprotected skin, measured on volunteers with product applied at **2 mg/cm²** (international method **ISO 24444**). SPF 15 blocks about 93% of UVB, SPF 30 about 97%, SPF 50 about 98%.
- **UVA-PF**: in vivo by persistent pigment darkening (PPD) or in vitro (ISO 24443) on roughened plates.
- **Critical wavelength (λc)**: the wavelength below which 90% of the area under the absorbance curve (290–400 nm) lies; λc ≥ 370 nm means broad spectrum (US rule).
- **PA system** (Japan, also used on Asian and many Indian products): PA+ (PPD 2 to < 4), PA++ (4 to < 8), PA+++ (8 to < 16), PA++++ (≥ 16).
- **Water resistance:** SPF re-tested after 40 or 80 minutes of immersion (US labels "water resistant (40 minutes)" or "(80 minutes)").
- **In vitro screening** (Mansur equation) is used in research and practicals, not for label claims.

### Regulatory aspects of sunscreens

| Region | Status and main rules |
| --- | --- |
| **India** | Sunscreens are **cosmetics** (no disease claim). They must meet the Cosmetics Rules, 2020 and BIS requirements on permitted ingredients and labelling; claims must not be false or misleading (Rule 36). Imported sunscreens need registration (COS-2) |
| **European Union** | Cosmetics. UV filters only from **Annex VI** of Regulation 1223/2009 with maximum concentrations. Commission Recommendation 2006/647/EC: UVA-PF at least **one third** of the labelled SPF and λc ≥ 370 nm; SPF bands **low (6–10), medium (15–25), high (30–50), very high (50+)**; no "sunblock" or "100% protection" claims; instructions to reapply |
| **USA** | **OTC drugs** under the FDA sunscreen monograph; limited list of filters; broad-spectrum test (λc ≥ 370 nm) needed to claim protection against skin cancer and early ageing; in 2019 the FDA proposed that only zinc oxide and titanium dioxide had enough data to be generally recognised as safe and effective and asked for more data on other filters |
| **Australia** | Primary sunscreens are therapeutic goods regulated by the TGA |
| **Japan** | Cosmetics or quasi-drugs; PA rating |

### Designing a sunscreen

1. **Filter selection** for broad spectrum: combine UVB and UVA filters (e.g. octinoxate + avobenzone + octocrylene, or bemotrizinol + zinc oxide), respecting permitted limits and avoiding unstable pairs (avobenzone degrades with octinoxate in light; photostabilisers are needed).
2. **SPF booster strategy**: film formers (acrylates copolymers), even distribution, light-scattering particles, synergy between filters.
3. **Vehicle**: o/w emulsions (most elegant), w/o (better water resistance), gels, sprays, sticks; solvent emollients (C12–15 alkyl benzoate) to dissolve crystalline filters and prevent recrystallisation.
4. **Physical filters**: coated (silica, alumina, dimethicone) to block photocatalysis; dispersed well to avoid whitening and clumping; for darker skin, tinting with iron oxides improves appearance and visible-light protection.
5. **Water resistance**: film-forming polymers, w/o or silicone-rich bases.
6. **Testing**: SPF, UVA-PF, λc, photostability, water resistance, phototoxicity and photoallergy screening, stability.
7. **Labelling**: SPF, UVA/PA, directions (apply generously 15–20 minutes before exposure, reapply every 2 hours and after swimming or sweating).

## 4.3 Addressing dry skin

**Goal:** restore water and lipids in the stratum corneum and normalise desquamation.

| Strategy | Actives |
| --- | --- |
| Humectants (pull water into the stratum corneum) | Glycerin (the gold standard), sodium PCA, urea (also keratolytic at higher levels), lactic acid/sodium lactate, hyaluronic acid, sorbitol, panthenol |
| Occlusives (reduce TEWL) | Petrolatum, mineral oil, dimethicone, lanolin, waxes, shea butter |
| Emollients (smooth the surface) | Esters, triglycerides, fatty alcohols |
| Barrier repair | Physiological lipid mixture of ceramides, cholesterol and free fatty acids, niacinamide (increases ceramide synthesis), phytosphingosine |
| Desquamation aid | Low-level AHAs (lactic acid), urea |
| Soothing | Allantoin, bisabolol, oat extract |

**Formulation:** w/o or rich o/w creams for very dry skin, lotions for body; avoid harsh surfactants in the regimen (syndet bar, cream cleanser); fragrance-free for sensitive skin; slightly acidic pH.

## 4.4 Addressing acne-prone skin

| Target | Cosmetic actives / approaches |
| --- | --- |
| Excess sebum | Oil-absorbing powders (silica, kaolin), zinc PCA, niacinamide |
| Follicular blockage (comedones) | Salicylic acid (lipophilic BHA, enters the follicle; exfoliant), glycolic/lactic acid, retinol and retinaldehyde (cosmetic retinoids), enzymes |
| C. acnes | Tea tree oil, zinc salts, azelaic acid (drug at therapeutic strengths in many markets) |
| Inflammation and marks | Niacinamide, licorice extract, allantoin, centella, sunscreen to prevent darkening of marks |

**Vehicle:** light, **non-comedogenic** gels, oil-free lotions, foaming cleansers with mild surfactants; avoid heavy occlusives and known comedogenic esters (isopropyl myristate in high amounts); add a non-greasy sunscreen. Medicated products with benzoyl peroxide, adapalene or antibiotics are drugs.

## 4.5 Addressing pigmentation

| Mechanism | Actives |
| --- | --- |
| Tyrosinase inhibition | Kojic acid, arbutin and alpha-arbutin (hydroquinone glucosides that release little hydroquinone), licorice extract (glabridin), azelaic acid, resorcinol derivatives (4-butylresorcinol), vitamin C (ascorbic acid and stable derivatives) |
| Blocking melanosome transfer | Niacinamide, soy extracts (protease inhibitors) |
| Reducing the inflammatory and UV signal | Antioxidants (vitamin C, vitamin E, ferulic acid), tranexamic acid (used topically in cosmetics in many markets) |
| Removing pigmented cells | AHAs, retinol, enzymes (exfoliation) |
| Prevention | **Broad-spectrum sunscreen plus visible-light protection** (iron oxides) – the single most important step, especially for melasma |

**Design points:** vitamin C (L-ascorbic acid) is stable only at low pH (about 3–3.5) and oxidises; use derivatives (magnesium ascorbyl phosphate, ascorbyl glucoside, ethyl ascorbic acid) or anhydrous/airless packs. Hydroquinone is a drug in India and banned in EU cosmetics; mercury compounds are prohibited except as in Rule 39(5). Claims must not promise "fairness" as a medical change in skin colour.

## 4.6 Addressing prickly heat and wrinkles

**Prickly heat (miliaria rubra):**

| Need | Approach |
| --- | --- |
| Keep skin dry and cool | Prickly-heat powders: talc (asbestos-free), starch, kaolin to absorb sweat |
| Cooling and itch relief | Menthol, camphor (low levels), calamine, zinc oxide |
| Reduce bacteria in ducts | Mild antimicrobial and astringent ingredients such as zinc salts (zinc oxide, zinc stearate); older antibacterials such as triclosan are now restricted in many markets |
| Avoid occlusion | Light lotions instead of heavy creams |

A typical prickly-heat powder: talc or starch base (absorbent, slip) + zinc oxide or calamine (soothing, mildly astringent) + kaolin (absorbs sweat) + menthol (cooling) + perfume. Safety: use cosmetic-grade, asbestos-free talc, and keep loose powders away from babies' faces to avoid inhalation.

**Wrinkles (anti-ageing):**

| Target | Actives |
| --- | --- |
| Prevent photoageing | Daily broad-spectrum sunscreen |
| Stimulate collagen, normalise epidermis | Retinol, retinaldehyde, retinyl esters (cosmetic retinoids; tretinoin is a drug) |
| Antioxidant protection | Vitamin C, vitamin E, ferulic acid, green tea polyphenols, coenzyme Q10, resveratrol |
| Signal and carrier peptides | Palmitoyl pentapeptide-4, copper tripeptide-1 |
| Exfoliation and texture | Glycolic acid, lactic acid, polyhydroxy acids (gluconolactone) |
| Hydration and plumping | Hyaluronic acid (various molecular weights), glycerin |
| Expression lines | Acetyl hexapeptide-8 (claimed to reduce muscle contraction signals) |

**Design points:** retinol is unstable to light, oxygen and heat → encapsulation, antioxidants, opaque airless packs, night use; acids are formulated at controlled pH for a balance of efficacy and irritation; start low and build up to reduce retinoid irritation.

## 4.7 Addressing body odour and dandruff

**Body odour – deodorants and antiperspirants**

| Product | Mechanism | Actives |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Deodorant | Reduce odour-forming bacteria; neutralise or mask odour | Antimicrobials (ethanol, triethyl citrate – esterase inhibitor, farnesol, zinc salts), odour absorbers (zinc ricinoleate, cyclodextrins), fragrance |
| Antiperspirant | Reduce sweat by forming temporary plugs of aluminium hydroxide gel in sweat ducts | Aluminium chlorohydrate, aluminium zirconium tetrachlorohydrex gly, aluminium chloride (stronger, more irritant) |

Formats: roll-on (aqueous or emulsion), stick (stearyl alcohol + volatile silicone), aerosol (powder in suspension), cream. Points: aluminium salts are acidic and can irritate; avoid use on broken skin; antiperspirants are drugs in the USA but cosmetics in India and the EU.

**Dandruff**

| Target | Actives |
| --- | --- |
| Malassezia (antifungal) | Zinc pyrithione, piroctone olamine, climbazole, selenium sulphide; ketoconazole and ciclopirox are drugs |
| Scaling | Salicylic acid, sulphur |
| Cytostatic | Selenium sulphide, coal tar (drug-type use) |
| Inflammation/itch | Menthol, zinc |

**Design:** anti-dandruff shampoos must **deposit and retain** the active on the scalp – insoluble zinc pyrithione particles of the right size are suspended with acrylate polymers and deposited with cationic polymers; contact time of a few minutes; use alternately with a mild shampoo; conditioners and leave-on tonics complete the regimen.

## 4.8 Addressing oral problems

| Problem | Mechanism targeted | Cosmeceutical actives |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Dental cavities** | Enamel demineralisation by plaque acids | **Fluoride** – sodium fluoride, sodium monofluorophosphate, stannous fluoride (≤ 1000 ppm fluoride in Indian toothpaste); fluoride forms fluorapatite/calcium fluoride reservoirs that resist acid and promote remineralisation; xylitol (non-fermentable sweetener); calcium phosphate technologies |
| **Bleeding gums** (gingivitis) | Plaque bacteria at the gum line | Antiplaque/antigingivitis agents: stannous fluoride, zinc citrate, cetylpyridinium chloride (mouthwash), essential oils (thymol, eucalyptol, menthol, methyl salicylate), chlorhexidine (a drug-strength mouthwash for short-term use), herbal (neem, clove) |
| **Mouth odour** (halitosis) | Volatile sulphur compounds from tongue bacteria | Zinc salts (bind sulphur), cetylpyridinium chloride, chlorine dioxide, flavours (mint) for masking; tongue cleaners |
| **Sensitive teeth** | Hydrodynamic stimulation of exposed dentine | **Nerve desensitisation**: potassium nitrate (potassium ions depolarise nerves); **tubule occlusion**: stannous fluoride, strontium salts, arginine with calcium carbonate, calcium sodium phosphosilicate (bioactive glass), hydroxyapatite; low-abrasivity pastes |
| **Tartar, stains, whitening** | Mineralised plaque, extrinsic stains | Pyrophosphates, zinc citrate (tartar control); silica abrasives, enzymes, peroxides (whitening within permitted limits) |

**Design points:** fluoride compatibility with abrasives (section 3.7); stannous fluoride needs stabilisation (anhydrous or chelated systems) and can stain; potassium nitrate works over 2–4 weeks of regular use; SLS-free pastes for people with mouth ulcers; flavour and sweetener make or break consumer use.

## 4.9 Evaluation of cosmeceuticals: safety, stability and efficacy

### Safety assessment

Because animal testing of cosmetics is banned in India and the EU, safety rests on **ingredient data + exposure + human-relevant tests**.

```text
Hazard data on each ingredient         Exposure in use
(toxicology literature, alternative    (amount applied, frequency,
 tests, supplier data)                  area, rinse-off/leave-on,
           │                            absorption) → Systemic exposure
           └──────────────┬─────────────dosage (SED)
                          ▼
            Margin of safety (MoS) = NOAEL ÷ SED
            (a MoS of at least 100 is generally taken as adequate)
                          ▼
     Product safety assessment report → human tests if needed
```

| Endpoint | Validated alternative (non-animal) methods |
| --- | --- |
| Skin irritation | Reconstructed human epidermis tests (OECD TG 439) |
| Skin corrosion | Reconstructed epidermis (OECD TG 431) |
| Eye irritation | Bovine corneal opacity and permeability (BCOP, OECD TG 437); reconstructed human cornea-like epithelium (OECD TG 492); HET-CAM (hen's egg chorioallantoic membrane, used for screening) |
| Skin sensitisation | Direct peptide reactivity assay (OECD TG 442C), KeratinoSens (442D), h-CLAT (442E), combined in defined approaches |
| Phototoxicity | 3T3 neutral red uptake phototoxicity test (OECD TG 432) |
| Genotoxicity | Ames test, in vitro micronucleus |
| Skin absorption | In vitro diffusion through human/pig skin (OECD TG 428, Franz cells) |

**Human tests (finished products, after safety is established):** single and repeated **patch tests**, the **human repeat insult patch test (HRIPT)** for sensitisation potential, use tests under dermatological supervision, ophthalmological tests for eye products, non-comedogenicity tests, in-use acceptability. India's **IS 4011:2018** gives methods of test for safety evaluation of cosmetics.

### Stability and microbiological quality

- **Stability:** real-time and accelerated storage (for example 40 °C/75% RH), freeze–thaw cycles, centrifugation, light exposure; checks on appearance, odour, colour, pH, viscosity, droplet/particle size, active content, packaging compatibility.
- **Microbiology:** total aerobic count and absence of specified pathogens per BIS limits; **challenge test** (ISO 11930).

### Efficacy and claim substantiation

| Claim | Measurement |
| --- | --- |
| Moisturisation | Corneometer (capacitance), skin conductance |
| Barrier repair | TEWL (Tewameter/evaporimeter) |
| Oil control | Sebumeter (photometric grease spot) |
| Firmness/elasticity | Cutometer (suction) |
| Wrinkles and texture | Fringe-projection 3D imaging, replica profilometry, standard photography with expert grading |
| Even tone, brightening | Chromameter (L\*a\*b\*), ITA°, Mexameter (melanin and erythema index), VISIA-type imaging |
| Sun protection | SPF (ISO 24444), UVA-PF, critical wavelength, water resistance |
| Anti-dandruff | Adherent scalp flaking score, Malassezia counts |
| Hair | Combing force, tensile strength, shine (goniophotometry), breakage |
| Oral | Plaque and gingival indices, fluoride uptake, Schiff sensitivity score, organoleptic halitosis scores, VSC meters |

Good claim substantiation uses a defined panel, controls (vehicle or untreated site), randomisation and blinding, and appropriate statistics. In India, claims must be truthful and not misleading (Rule 36), and the industry self-regulatory code of the Advertising Standards Council of India (ASCI) asks for evidence behind advertised claims.

## Remember

- Cosmeceutical design = biology → active (permitted level, pH, stability) → vehicle and delivery → safety → proof. Treatment claims make it a drug.
- UVB 290–320 nm (burn), UVA2 320–340, UVA1 340–400 nm (ageing, pigment); visible light worsens melasma.
- Sunscreens: organic (cinnamates, salicylates, benzophenones, avobenzone, octocrylene, triazines) vs inorganic (ZnO, TiO2); SPF at 2 mg/cm² (ISO 24444); λc ≥ 370 nm; UVA-PF ≥ ⅓ SPF (EU); PA+ to PA++++; India = cosmetic, USA = OTC drug, EU = Annex VI filters.
- Dry skin: humectant + occlusive + emollient + barrier lipids. Acne: salicylic acid, niacinamide, non-comedogenic vehicle. Pigmentation: tyrosinase inhibitors + niacinamide + sunscreen. Wrinkles: retinol, antioxidants, peptides, AHAs, sunscreen.
- Prickly heat: absorbent cooling powders, avoid occlusion. Body odour: deodorant (antimicrobial, fragrance) vs antiperspirant (aluminium salts plug ducts). Dandruff: zinc pyrithione, piroctone olamine, climbazole, selenium sulphide.
- Caries: fluoride (≤ 1000 ppm India); gums: stannous fluoride, zinc, CPC, essential oils; halitosis: zinc, CPC, ClO2; sensitivity: potassium nitrate (nerve) or tubule occluders.
- Safety: MoS = NOAEL/SED ≥ 100; OECD alternatives 439, 431, 437, 492, 442C/D/E, 432, 428; HRIPT; IS 4011:2018. Efficacy: corneometer, TEWL, sebumeter, cutometer, chromameter, profilometry.
